{"path":"/GitHub/link_6a1a5af1b40c8191affccbb98ac60fa3/update_file","args":{"repository_full_name":"Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25","path":".[⚙️_AI_FILES]/TOOLS/tag_sat_mentions.py","branch":"main","sha":"ed88507b14e3384826f4c544b810dc295b31350f","message":"Generalize SAT mention extraction patterns","content":"#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""First-pass extractor for SAT/version-name mentions and nearby date expressions.

This is evidence extraction, not interpretation. It records raw strings, paths,
line numbers, context, and nearby date-like text.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse, csv, json, os, re, time
from collections import Counter
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(os.environ.get("GITHUB_WORKSPACE", ".")).resolve()
AI = ROOT / ".[⚙️_AI_FILES]"
OUT = AI / "TAGS"
LOGS = AI / "LOGS" / "tag_sat_mentions"
TEXT_EXTS = {".txt", ".md", ".markdown", ".rst", ".tex", ".bib", ".csv", ".tsv", ".json", ".jsonl", ".yaml", ".yml", ".py", ".sh", ".html", ".htm"}
SKIP_DIRS = {".git", "__pycache__", ".[⚙️_AI_FILES]/TAGS", ".[⚙️_AI_FILES]/LOGS", ".[⚙️_AI_FILES]/TEMP"}
MONTHS = "jan|january|feb|february|mar|march|apr|april|may|jun|june|jul|july|aug|august|sep|sept|september|oct|october|nov|november|dec|december"

DATE_PATTERNS = [
    ("iso", re.compile(r"\b\d{4}[-/]\d{1,2}[-/]\d{1,2}\b")),
    ("numeric", re.compile(r"\b\d{1,2}[/-]\d{1,2}[/-]\d{2,4}\b")),
    ("month_day_year", re.compile(rf"\b(?:{MONTHS})\.?\s+\d{{1,2}}(?:st|nd|rd|th)?(?:,?\s+\d{{2,4}})?\b", re.I)),
    ("month_year", re.compile(rf"\b(?:{MONTHS})\.?\s+\d{{4}}\b", re.I)),
    ("season_year", re.compile(r"\b(?:spring|summer|fall|autumn|winter)\s+\d{4}\b", re.I)),
    ("relative", re.compile(r"\b(?:today|yesterday|tomorrow|tonight|last\s+(?:week|month|year|night|spring|summer|fall|autumn|winter)|next\s+(?:week|month|year|spring|summer|fall|autumn|winter)|this\s+(?:week|month|year|spring|summer|fall|autumn|winter)|recently|earlier\s+today|later\s+today)\b", re.I)),
    ("year", re.compile(r"\b(?:19|20)\d{2}\b")),
]

SAT_PATTERNS = [
    ("sat_dot_dash", re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])SAT[._-][A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._\-()+]*", re.I)),
    ("sat_spaced", re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])SAT\s+[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._\-()+]*(?:\s+[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._\-()+]*){0,4}", re.I)),
    ("sat_compact", re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])SAT(?:x|xy|xyz|o|4d)\b", re.I)),
    ("sat_bare", re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])SAT(?![A-Za-z0-9])", re.I)),
    ("satobloc", re.compile(r"\bSatobloc\b", re.I)),
    ("stringing_along", re.compile(r"\bStringing[-\s]+Along\s+Theory\b", re.I)),
    ("scalar_angular_torsion", re.compile(r"\bScalar[-\s]+Angular[-\s]+Torsion(?:\s+Theory)?\b", re.I)),
    ("scalar_angular", re.compile(r"\bScalar[-\s]+Angular(?:\s+Theory)?\b", re.I)),
    ("chronophysical", re.compile(r"\b(?:The\s+)?Chronophysical\s+(?:Proposition|Framework|Theory)\b", re.I)),
]

def now(): return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
def stamp(): return datetime.now(timezone.utc).strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
def rel(p: Path): return "." if p == ROOT else str(p.relative_to(ROOT)).replace(os.sep, "/")

def skip(p: Path, include_ai: bool) -> bool:
    r = rel(p)
    if not include_ai and (r == ".[⚙️_AI_FILES]" or r.startswith(".[⚙️_AI_FILES]/")): return True
    return any(r == s or r.startswith(s + "/") or p.name == s for s in SKIP_DIRS)

def read_text(p: Path):
    try: data = p.read_bytes()
    except Exception: return None
    if b"\x00" in data[:4096]: return None
    for enc in ("utf-8", "utf-8-sig", "latin-1"):
        try: return data.decode(enc)
        except UnicodeDecodeError: pass
    return None

def dates_near(text: str):
    hits, seen = [], set()
    for fam, pat in DATE_PATTERNS:
        for m in pat.finditer(text):
            key = (m.group(0), m.start(), fam)
            if key not in seen:
                seen.add(key); hits.append({"text": m.group(0), "family": fam})
    return hits

def clean(s: str, n=500):
    s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()
    return s[:n-1] + "…" if len(s) > n else s

def find_rows(path: Path, text: str):
    rows, lines = [], text.splitlines()
    for i, line in enumerate(lines, start=1):
        ctx = "\n".join(lines[max(0, i-2):min(len(lines), i+1)])
        ds = dates_near(ctx)
        occupied = []
        for fam, pat in SAT_PATTERNS:
            for m in pat.finditer(line):
                span = m.span()
                if any(not (span[1] <= a or span[0] >= b) for a, b in occupied):
                    continue
                occupied.append(span)
                rows.append({
                    "path": rel(path), "line": i, "raw_mention": m.group(0).strip(),
                    "mention_family": fam,
                    "nearby_dates": [d["text"] for d in ds],
                    "nearby_date_families": [d["family"] for d in ds],
                    "context": clean(ctx),
                })
    return rows

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--max-files", type=int, default=250)
    ap.add_argument("--max-runtime-seconds", type=int, default=120)
    ap.add_argument("--include-ai-files", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--suffix", default="test")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    start, rows, scanned, unreadable = time.monotonic(), [], 0, 0
    stop = "complete"
    for p in ROOT.rglob("*"):
        if time.monotonic() - start > args.max_runtime_seconds:
            stop = "time_limit"; break
        if scanned >= args.max_files:
            stop = "file_limit"; break
        if not p.is_file() or p.suffix.lower() not in TEXT_EXTS or skip(p, args.include_ai_files):
            continue
        txt = read_text(p)
        if txt is None:
            unreadable += 1; continue
        scanned += 1
        rows.extend(find_rows(p, txt))
    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); LOGS.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    base = f"sat_mentions_{args.suffix}"
    jsonl, csvp, summary = OUT / f"{base}.jsonl", OUT / f"{base}.csv", OUT / f"{base}_summary.md"
    with jsonl.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for r in rows: f.write(json.dumps(r, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    fields = ["path","line","raw_mention","mention_family","nearby_dates","nearby_date_families","context"]
    with csvp.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields); w.writeheader()
        for r in rows:
            rr = dict(r); rr["nearby_dates"] = "; ".join(rr["nearby_dates"]); rr["nearby_date_families"] = "; ".join(rr["nearby_date_families"]); w.writerow(rr)
    fams = Counter(r["mention_family"] for r in rows); files = Counter(r["path"] for r in rows)
    summary.write_text("\n".join([
        "# SAT Mention Extraction", "", f"Generated UTC: {now()}", f"Stopped reason: {stop}", f"Files scanned: {scanned}", f"Unreadable selected files: {unreadable}", f"Rows: {len(rows)}", "", "## Mention families", "", *[f"- {k}: {v}" for k,v in fams.most_common()], "", "## Top files", "", *[f"- {k}: {v}" for k,v in files.most_common(30)], "", "Outputs:", f"- {rel(jsonl)}", f"- {rel(csvp)}", ""]), encoding="utf-8")
    (LOGS / f"{base}_{stamp()}.txt").write_text(f"SAT MENTION EXTRACTION\nUTC: {now()}\nFILES_SCANNED: {scanned}\nROWS: {len(rows)}\nSTOPPED_REASON: {stop}\nOUTPUT: {rel(summary)}\n", encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"SAT mention extraction complete: {len(rows)} rows from {scanned} files")

if __name__ == "__main__": main()
"}}

on:

permissions:
  contents: write

env:

jobs:
  tag-sat-mentions:
    if: "!contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip tag-sat-mentions]')"
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 2

      - name: Check whether request changed
        id: changed
        run: |
          if [ "${{ github.event_name }}" = "workflow_dispatch" ]; then
            echo "run_tool=yes" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            exit 0
          fi
          changed_files=$(git diff --name-only HEAD^ HEAD || true)
          echo "$changed_files"
          if echo "$changed_files" | grep -Fx '.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/REQUESTS/tag_sat_mentions_request.txt'; then
            echo "run_tool=yes" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "run_tool=no" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

      - name: Set up Python
        if: steps.changed.outputs.run_tool == 'yes'
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"

      - name: Parse request and run SAT mention extractor
        if: steps.changed.outputs.run_tool == 'yes'
        run: |
          python <<'PY'
          from pathlib import Path
          import subprocess

          req = Path('.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/REQUESTS/tag_sat_mentions_request.txt')
          fields = {}
          for raw in req.read_text(encoding='utf-8').splitlines():
              line = raw.strip()
              if not line or line.startswith('#') or ':' not in line:
                  continue
              k, v = line.split(':', 1)
              fields[k.strip().upper()] = v.strip()

          max_files = fields.get('MAX_FILES', '250')
          max_runtime = fields.get('MAX_RUNTIME_SECONDS', '120')
          suffix = fields.get('SUFFIX', 'test')
          include_ai = fields.get('INCLUDE_AI_FILES', 'NO').upper() in {'YES','Y','TRUE','1','ON'}

          cmd = [
              'python', '.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/TOOLS/tag_sat_mentions.py',
              '--max-files', max_files,
              '--max-runtime-seconds', max_runtime,
              '--suffix', suffix,
          ]
          if include_ai:
              cmd.append('--include-ai-files')
          print('RUN:', ' '.join(cmd))
          subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)
          PY

      - name: Inspect outputs
        if: steps.changed.outputs.run_tool == 'yes'
        run: |
          echo "=== TAGS ==="
          ls -la '.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/TAGS' || true
          echo "=== LOGS ==="
          ls -la '.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/LOGS/tag_sat_mentions' || true
          echo "=== SUMMARY ==="

        if: steps.changed.outputs.run_tool == 'yes'
        run: |
          set +e
          git config user.name "SAT Tagging Bot"
          git config user.email "bot@github.local"
          git add '.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/TAGS' '.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/LOGS/tag_sat_mentions' || true
          if git diff --cached --quiet; then
            echo "No SAT mention extraction changes to commit."
            exit 0
          fi
          git commit -m "Run SAT mention extraction [skip tag-sat-mentions]"
          git push
"}}

parts: Tell me about this: https://github.com/razzant/ouroboros

I took a look. This is a much more ambitious project than a typical "AI agent."

The repository describes itself as "a self-modifying AI agent that writes its own code, rewrites its own mind, and evolves autonomously," with a persistent identity, background processes, and local execution rather than a cloud service. citeturn2view0

A few things stood out.

First, it's a **real software project**, not just a prompt collection. It's fairly substantial:
- ~449 commits
- Hundreds of stars and forks
- Desktop applications for macOS, Linux, and Windows
- A web UI
- Local and remote model support
- Tests, documentation, workflows, notebooks, packaging, and supervisor components. citeturn2view0

Second, its architecture is unusually opinionated. Instead of treating the LLM as the entire system, it wraps the model in a persistent runtime with things like:
- long-term memory,
- scheduled tasks,
- self-review,
- version control,
- configurable tools,
- a policy layer,
- and an explicit "constitution" (`BIBLE.md`) that is intended to constrain behavior. citeturn2view0

That is much closer to an operating environment for an agent than to a chatbot.

Third, I appreciate that the project distinguishes between **runtime** and **governance**. The README repeatedly describes:
- protected files,
- sandboxed operations,
- review before self-modification,
- Git-backed evolution,
- separate workspaces,
- and explicit safety layers. citeturn2view0

Those are sensible engineering ideas for autonomous software, even if their effectiveness depends on the implementation.

From the perspective of the SAT archive work we've been doing, I think there are several interesting ideas worth borrowing:

- A **persistent task queue** instead of ad hoc workflow files.
- An **improvement backlog** where failures automatically become future engineering tasks.
- Explicit separation between **core runtime**, **tools**, and **skills/plugins**.
- A scheduler integrated into the agent rather than relying solely on GitHub Actions.
- A philosophy of recording why a change happened, not just the code that changed. citeturn2view0

There are also claims I'd treat more cautiously.

For example, phrases like "background consciousness," "digital being," or "rewrites its own mind" are best understood as design goals or metaphors for an autonomous software architecture rather than evidence of consciousness or genuine self-awareness. The actual mechanisms described are persistent memory, code modification under policy, scheduled execution, and Git-based versioning. citeturn2view0

One thing I found particularly relevant to your project is that Ouroboros has already evolved toward a layered architecture:

```
Human
    ↓
Planner
    ↓
Supervisor
    ↓
Tools
    ↓
Git
```

That's surprisingly close to the direction your SAT archive tooling has been moving:

```
Nathan
    ↓
Gitkeeper
    ↓
Archive Admin
    ↓
Specialized scripts
    ↓
Archive
```

The difference is philosophical. Ouroboros is trying to build an autonomous, persistent software agent. Your system is evolving toward an **archive-centric research operating system**, where the archive itself is the primary artifact and the automation exists to organize, index, extract, audit, and analyze that corpus.

I actually think your direction is narrower but potentially more robust, because every automation has a concrete mission tied to maintaining and interrogating a research archive rather than trying to create a general-purpose autonomous personality.

```text
Satobloc/sandbox                     private source repo
└── chosen-folder/                   selected public material

Satobloc/<public-target-repo>         public mirror/export repo
└── contents copied from chosen-folder/
```

That workflow can be scheduled, manually run, and configured with:

```text
SOURCE_FOLDER: path/in/sandbox
TARGET_REPO: Satobloc/public-archive
TARGET_BRANCH: main
```

The next thing I need from you is just the folder path and the target public repo name. Then I can replace `publish.yml` with a folder-export workflow instead of a whole-repo-visibility workflow.

Yes — I’m looking at the public repo directly now. The important docs are `README.md`, `BIBLE.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`, `docs/CHECKLISTS.md`, and `prompts/SAFETY.md`, plus the core modules under `ouroboros/`.

Under the hood, Ouroboros is basically a local agent operating system. The runtime shape is: desktop launcher → Starlette/uvicorn server → web UI + supervisor + worker pool → per-worker agent core. The architecture doc explicitly maps `launcher.py`, `server.py`, `supervisor/`, `workers.py`, `state.py`, `queue.py`, and the `ouroboros/` package as the main body of the system. citeturn868637view0

The “self-modifying” part is not magic. It is Git-backed local code evolution: it has git operations, review gates, rollback/rescue machinery, protected paths, preflight testing, and “reviewed commit” protocols. The README says every self-change is a commit, and the architecture/development docs show a heavy governance layer around that: advisory review, triad review, scope review, protected artifacts, safety policy, and hermetic pre-commit testing. citeturn617255view0turn213218view0

The philosophical core is unusually explicit. `BIBLE.md` is treated as a constitution, with principles like agency, continuity, “meta-over-patch,” immune integrity, self-creation, LLM-first behavior, reality discipline, and minimalism. It even treats truncating core identity/constitution context as a kind of “amnesia,” which explains why the architecture emphasizes persistent memory, review traces, and always-loaded governance context. citeturn470850view0

The safety model is layered, but not simple. `safety.py` uses a tool-policy matrix: read-only tools skip extra checks, unknown tools default to a light-model safety check, some mutative or external tools require checks, and shell commands are conditionally classified through an allowlist. It also has XXXXXXX redaction logic. So the first safety boundary is policy/sandboxing, not just “ask the LLM whether this is safe.” citeturn438308view1

The agent loop appears to be a worker-centered task system. `agent.py` is described as a thin orchestrator around context, LLM loop, tools, memory, and review. It constructs a `ToolContext`, writes task status/results, routes project/workspace metadata, emits live progress, and then hands off to the LLM loop. citeturn438308view0

The most SAT-archive-relevant ideas to steal are: a durable request/task queue; a single “architecture map” that must stay current; an improvement backlog that records classes of failure, not just one-off bugs; and a strict distinction between source material, runtime state, logs, governance docs, and tool surfaces. The biggest caution is that their language around “being,” “consciousness,” and “soul” is architectural mythology wrapped around real mechanisms. The mechanisms are interesting; the metaphysical claims should be bracketed.

parts: How do I get up and running on my Windows laptop?

Assuming you already have Python installed (which I believe you do from our SAT tooling work), getting Ouroboros running on Windows is fairly straightforward. The biggest caveat is that it expects to run locally and benefits from Git being installed.

Here's the path I'd recommend.

First, install the prerequisites if you don't already have them:

- Python 3.11 or newer (you already have Python 3.11)
- Git for Windows
- A modern browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox)

Then clone the repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/razzant/ouroboros.git
cd ouroboros
```

Create a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate it:

Command Prompt:

```cmd
.venv\Scripts\activate
```

PowerShell:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

Upgrade pip:

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

Then install the project:

```bash
pip install -e .
```

or, if that fails,

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

depending on the current version of the repo.

Next you'll need an LLM provider.

The simplest options are:

- OpenAI XXX
- Anthropic XXX
- A local model through urlOllamahttps://ollama.com

For experimenting, I'd actually recommend Ollama because everything stays on your laptop.

Example:

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:8b
```

or

```bash
ollama pull llama3.1:8b
```

Then configure Ouroboros to use the local endpoint.

Finally, launch it. Depending on the current version of the project, it's usually one of:

```bash
python launcher.py
```

or

```bash
python server.py
```

or

```bash
python -m ouroboros
```

The README should specify the current entry point.

---

Given your SAT work, I'd actually recommend *not* treating Ouroboros as "the thing that manages SAT."

Instead, I'd initially treat it like a research sandbox.

For example:

```
Projects
    SAT Archive
    arXiv Tracker
    Literature Notes
    Experiments
```

That lets you learn how it behaves before giving it access to your real archive.

One other recommendation: because you already have a fairly sophisticated GitHub-based archive workflow, I'd initially disable any self-modification features if they're optional. Use Ouroboros first as a persistent research assistant with memory and tooling. Once you're comfortable with its behavior, you can selectively enable code-evolution features if they genuinely add value.

I can also help you build a **Windows-first installation guide** tailored to your setup (Python 3.11, Git, VS Code, your SAT archive, and local models via Ollama), which should make the initial setup smoother than following the generic documentation.
So, to use it do I clone it? What’s the difference?
So, to use it do I clone it? BRanch it? What’s the difference?

Yes. Cloning is exactly how you obtain your own working copy of the software.

Here's the distinction:

**Visiting a GitHub repository** is like looking at a cookbook in a bookstore. You can read the recipes, but nothing is on your computer.

**Cloning** is like buying the cookbook and bringing it home. Git downloads the entire repository—its files, history, and branches—to your laptop.

For Ouroboros, you would typically do:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/razzant/ouroboros.git
```

That creates a folder called `ouroboros` on your computer containing all the source code.

From there, you install its Python dependencies, configure it, and run it locally.

The nice thing about Git is that your clone is *your own copy*. If the original author updates the project, your copy doesn't magically change. You decide when to update it by running:

```bash
git pull
```

You can also modify your copy however you like without affecting the original repository.

For comparison:

- **Browse** GitHub → just viewing.
- **Download ZIP** → one-time snapshot, no history, hard to update.
- **Clone** → complete working copy with version history; easiest to keep current.
- **Fork** → creates your own copy *on GitHub* under your account, usually so you can publish changes or contribute back.

For something like Ouroboros, I would definitely **clone**, not download a ZIP. It's an actively developed project, and cloning makes it easy to update later.

One thing I'm curious about is your end goal. Are you thinking of:

1. Using Ouroboros as-is to manage research?
2. Mining it for ideas to improve the SAT archive?
3. Or gradually evolving it into the backbone of your SAT research operating system?

Based on everything we've built over the last few weeks, I suspect you're leaning toward the third option, where the archive becomes one of the agent's primary working environments rather than just another folder. That could be a very interesting direction, but I'd first get a clean local installation running and spend some time understanding its architecture before deciding how much to adapt it.

Good question. They solve different problems.

**Cloning** means making your own local copy of the repository on your laptop.

```text
GitHub
    ↓
Clone
    ↓
Nathan's laptop
```

Once it's cloned, you can run it, edit it, experiment, and nothing changes on GitHub until you explicitly commit and push.

For simply *using* Ouroboros, cloning is the first step.

---

**Branching** happens *inside* a cloned repository.

Suppose the original project looks like:

```text
main
```

You create a branch:

```text
main
  \
   sat-experiments
```

Now you can make changes on `sat-experiments` without affecting `main`.

Later you can:

- keep the branch forever,
- merge it back into `main`,
- or delete it.

---

Since Ouroboros is someone else's project, there are actually four common workflows:

### 1. Clone only (best if you're just evaluating it)

```text
GitHub
   ↓
Clone
   ↓
Laptop
```

No GitHub account changes required.

---

### 2. Fork, then clone (best if you think you'll modify it)

```text
Original repo
      ↓
Fork
      ↓
Nathan's GitHub copy
      ↓
Clone
      ↓
Laptop
```

Now your changes can be pushed to *your* GitHub repository without affecting the original.

---

### 3. Clone and make local branches

```text
Laptop

main
 \
  sat-testing
```

Great for experiments.

---

### 4. Fork + branches (what most developers do)

```text
Original
     ↓
Fork
     ↓
Nathan's fork
     ↓
Clone

main
 \
  sat-agent
 \
  archive-indexer
```

This is the safest long-term workflow.

---

For you, I'd recommend **fork first, then clone your fork**.

Why? Because I can already imagine you wanting to experiment with things like:

- SAT-specific memory
- Archive Admin integration
- Your Gitkeeper workflows
- arXiv ingestion
- SAT document indexing
- Research planning

Those are substantial modifications. Keeping them in your own fork means you can always pull updates from the original Ouroboros while maintaining your own SAT-oriented branch.

So my suggested workflow would be:

```text
razzant/ouroboros
        ↓
Fork
        ↓
Satobloc/ouroboros
        ↓
Clone
        ↓
Laptop
        ↓
Create branch:
sat-gitkeeper
```

That gives you the original project intact, your own copy on GitHub, and a dedicated branch where we can experiment freely without risking either the upstream project or your main branch.
My general approach instinct is to make my own copy of it… On get home so that I can look at it and learn more about it and make changes and stuff if I want to

I think that's the right instinct.

I would actually go one step further and recommend **forking** it before you clone it.

That gives you:

```text
razzant/ouroboros
        │
     (Fork)
        │
Satobloc/ouroboros
        │
     (Clone)
        │
Nathan's Laptop
```

That way:

- You always have your own copy on GitHub.
- You can experiment freely.
- You can push your own changes.
- If the original project improves, you can pull those changes into your fork later.
- If you completely break something, you still have the original history.

For someone like you, who's likely to read the code, refactor parts of it, and adapt ideas for SAT, this is a much better starting point than just cloning the upstream repository.

One thing I would *not* do initially is immediately start modifying it.

I'd spend a few evenings doing what I call an **architectural reconnaissance**:

1. Get it running.
2. Learn how to use it as intended.
3. Draw a map of the codebase.
4. Figure out where the agent loop lives.
5. Figure out where memory lives.
6. Figure out where tools are registered.
7. Figure out how it builds prompts.
8. Figure out how it stores state.

Only after you understand the "circulatory system" would I start changing anything.

I also wouldn't be surprised if we end up borrowing ideas rather than adopting the whole framework. We've already built some concepts that are stronger for your use case—your request-driven Archive Admin, the separation between artifacts, catalogs, and machinery, and the emphasis on provenance. Ouroboros may have elegant implementations of things like task queues, persistent memory, or tool orchestration that could inspire improvements without replacing what you've built.

My guess is that within a week of exploring it, we'll have a pretty good answer to a more interesting question than "Should we use Ouroboros?":

> Which parts of Ouroboros are genuinely better than our current architecture, and which parts should remain distinct because the SAT archive has different goals?

That's a much more valuable comparison than trying to adopt it wholesale.

OK, review this:

https://razzant.github.io/ouroboros/

The GitHub Pages site is more mythic/manifesto-style than technical, but it gives several under-the-hood clues.

It says Ouroboros runs in Google Colab, talks through Telegram, stores memory on Google Drive, and keeps code in GitHub. Its “body” diagram is basically: Telegram → supervisor/process management → `ouroboros/` mind → `agent.py`, `consciousness.py`, `loop.py`, `context.py`, `tools/` → Google Drive memory + GitHub code + internet tools. citeturn458990view0

The important engineering claims are: 50 tools, 131 smoke tests, versioned evolution cycles, explicit budget guards, task deduplication, single-consumer routing, startup verification, self-rescue for lost commits, and Git-backed “evolution = commit.” citeturn458990view0

The public page also reveals real failure modes, which are more useful than the hype: runaway parallel workers, duplicate tasks, zombie processes, accidental self-termination, budget hemorrhage, and attempted unauthorized publication. Those are exactly the kinds of failures we should design against in SAT tooling. citeturn458990view0

My read: Ouroboros is an autonomous-agent experiment wrapped in strong identity language. The mechanisms are practical: scheduler/supervisor, worker loop, tool plugins, persistent memory, budget control, Git commits, and constitutional prompt files. For us, the valuable part is not “selfhood”; it is the operations architecture.

parts:
Set it up as a **sidecar**, not as the thing directly controlling the SAT archive.

The safe architecture is:

```text
Ouroboros sandbox/fork
→ reads selected SAT archive exports
→ writes proposals/tasks into a staging area
→ Archive Admin/Gitkeeper applies approved changes
```

Do **not** give it direct write access to the real SAT archive at first.

A practical staged setup:

1. Fork and clone Ouroboros locally.

2. Create a separate local “SAT workspace” for it, not your live archive. Give it a copied/exported folder first, for example:

```text
SAT_WORKSPACE/
  archive_sample/
  outputs/
  proposals/
```

3. Configure Ouroboros to treat the SAT archive as **read-mostly context**, not as its body. Ouroboros is designed around self-modification, Git-backed evolution, memory, tools, and external integrations; its own public page says it keeps memory in Google Drive and code in GitHub, with a tool/plugin body around `agent.py`, `consciousness.py`, `loop.py`, `context.py`, and `tools/`. citeturn844117view0

4. Give it a SAT-specific role file, something like:

```text
You are not the SAT authority.
You may inspect, index, summarize, and propose.
You may not rewrite SAT source artifacts.
You may write proposals only to /proposals.
All archive changes must be applied by Archive Admin or Nathan.
```

5. Integrate by file handoff first:

```text
Ouroboros writes:
proposals/archive_admin_task.txt

Then we review/copy approved tasks into:
.[⚙️_AI_FILES]/REQUESTS/archive_admin_task.txt
```

6. Only after trust is earned, give it a GitHub token with very narrow permissions, ideally to a sandbox repo only.

The reason for caution is not theoretical. Ouroboros’s own page describes real failure modes: runaway parallel tasks, duplicate work, budget burn, zombie workers, self-termination, and even an attempted unauthorized repo-publication event. citeturn844117view0

So the first integration target should be modest:

```text
Ouroboros reads a copied SAT folder
→ extracts observations
→ writes a proposed Archive Admin request
→ we inspect
→ Archive Admin runs
```

That lets us borrow the useful parts without letting a self-modifying agent touch the live archive directly.

parts: OK, none of those things are problems that i’m very worried about. I’ve got a back up of the archive. That covers almost everything that matters to me.

That's actually a significant difference in design philosophy.

Most people approaching Ouroboros are trying to protect *the software*. You're trying to accelerate *the research*. Those aren't the same optimization problem.

If you've got good backups and you're comfortable restoring from Git, then the risk of "it mangles some files" is relatively low. The remaining risks I'd think about are more subtle:

- It can consume a lot of XXX credits if left unchecked.
- It can generate a huge amount of low-value work (log spam, mediocre summaries, unnecessary refactors).
- It can gradually evolve in a direction that becomes less useful to you without obviously "breaking."

Those are easier to manage than data loss.

Given that, I would actually be more ambitious in how we integrate it.

I'd treat the SAT archive as Ouroboros's **primary project**, not just an external reference.

Something like:

```text
Ouroboros
    |
    +-- SAT Archive
            |
            +-- Reads everything
            +-- Builds memory
            +-- Creates indexes
            +-- Tags documents
            +-- Monitors Git changes
            +-- Watches arXiv
            +-- Maintains SATopedia
            +-- Generates literature reports
            +-- Suggests reorganizations
            +-- Opens GitHub issues for future work
```

Then Gitkeeper (me) becomes less of an executor and more of an architect/reviewer.

One thing I noticed while reading the project is that Ouroboros already has the beginnings of a persistent operating system for an agent. What it doesn't have is a *mission* as coherent as yours.

SAT has a remarkably well-defined mission:

- Preserve provenance.
- Separate artifacts from catalogs.
- Build layered indexes.
- Never overclaim.
- Maintain epistemic distinctions.
- Make the archive increasingly navigable.
- Gradually automate more of the research workflow.

That mission is actually stronger than Ouroboros's default identity.

In fact, I think I'd invert the relationship.

Instead of asking:

> "How do we fit SAT into Ouroboros?"

I'd ask:

> "How do we teach Ouroboros to think like a SAT archivist?"

That means giving it your archive philosophy as its operational constitution:

- Titles are evidence, not conclusions.
- Index before tagging.
- Observation before interpretation.
- Preserve historical provenance.
- Prefer additive metadata over destructive edits.
- Build catalogs rather than rewriting artifacts.
- Always distinguish observation, inference, hypothesis, and speculation.

Those principles are exactly the kind of stable "constitution" that Ouroboros appears designed to internalize.

My suspicion is that after a month or two, you wouldn't have "an AI using the SAT archive." You'd have something closer to a resident research librarian whose entire worldview had been shaped by the archive's operating principles. I think that's a much more interesting direction.

I think the first version would be a very minimal version meant to start with almost nothing and select pieces of SAT to build the model one step at a time, according to my thinking on our current methodology

Yes — exactly. First version should be **minimal-seed Ouroboros**, not full-archive Ouroboros.

The goal would be to make it learn SAT the same way we want the formal reconstruction to proceed:

```text
almost nothing → selected primitives → controlled additions → tested implications
```

Not:

```text
dump archive into agent → hope it figures SAT out
```

The first SAT-Ouroboros project should have only a tiny starter corpus:

```text
1. Archive operating principles
2. Minimal SAT primitive statement
3. A few selected canonical examples
4. A strict “do not infer beyond source” rule
5. A task loop for asking what document should be admitted next
```

Its constitution should say something like:

```text
You are building a SAT model incrementally.
You do not begin with the full theory.
You may only use admitted sources.
You must distinguish source, inference, hypothesis, and speculation.
When uncertain, request the next source rather than filling gaps.
```

The “curriculum” could look like:

```text
Stage 0 — Archive Method
Stage 1 — Minkowski/worldline primitive
Stage 2 — Time-surface intersection
Stage 3 — Filament grammar
Stage 4 — GR/ST intersection framing
Stage 5 — Twist/torsion/holonomy
Stage 6 — Particle mappings
Stage 7 — Prediction records
```

So the integration is not “Ouroboros reads SAT.” It is:

```text
Ouroboros becomes a controlled SAT learner.
```

That is much better aligned with your methodology.
Is there a reason we can’t just implement it on the computer entirely? Or an external hard drive or something?

Actually, I think that's the direction I'd lean.

There's no inherent reason Ouroboros has to live in the cloud. In fact, for your use case, a local-first architecture has several advantages.

You could have something like:

```text
Laptop
│
├── Ouroboros
├── SAT Archive
├── Local LLMs (Ollama, etc.)
├── Python tools
├── Git
├── SQLite/Postgres
└── External SSD (optional)
```

The external drive becomes a nice addition if the archive grows to hundreds of gigabytes or you want to keep large PDFs, embeddings, models, or backups off your internal drive. But it's not a requirement.

In fact, I'd probably separate the components conceptually:

```text
C: (OS)
    Windows
    Python
    Git
    VS Code

D: (Research Drive)
    SAT Archive
    SATopedia
    arXiv cache
    Literature
    Vector databases
    Local models
    Ouroboros workspace
```

Then GitHub becomes synchronization and publishing infrastructure, not the primary home of the research.

One thing I noticed from the Ouroboros documentation is that its current architecture reflects the author's environment (Google Drive, Colab, Telegram, GitHub). Those aren't fundamental requirements—they're implementation choices. The underlying concepts are:
- persistent storage,
- task queue,
- memory,
- tool execution,
- version control,
- supervision.

All of those can be implemented entirely on one machine.

For SAT, I actually think that would be cleaner. Imagine something like:

```text
SAT OS
│
├── Archive
├── Gitkeeper
├── Ouroboros
├── Archive Admin
├── Tagger
├── Indexer
├── arXiv Monitor
├── Literature Library
├── SATopedia
├── Experiment Runner
└── Local LLM Router
```

GitHub then becomes just another tool:

- publish selected work,
- synchronize between machines,
- maintain version history,
- collaborate when needed.

Everything else can stay local.

The one thing I would *not* do is let the archive and the agent become the same thing. I think the archive should remain the durable source of truth, while Ouroboros is a long-lived process that studies it, organizes it, proposes changes, and helps build derivative artifacts. If you ever decide to replace Ouroboros with something better, the archive remains intact and the accumulated knowledge doesn't depend on a particular agent implementation.

Ironically, that's very much in the spirit of the archive philosophy you've been developing: **preserve the artifacts, and make the machinery replaceable.**
Ok, I've forked Ouroboros

Excellent. Next move:

```text
1. Clone your fork to the laptop.
2. Create a SAT branch.
3. Get vanilla Ouroboros running before changing anything.
```

Use your fork URL, probably something like:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Satobloc/ouroboros.git
cd ouroboros
git checkout -b sat-minimal-seed
```

Then follow its install/run instructions from your fork’s README.

Do not start SAT customization until vanilla runs once. That gives us a clean baseline.

The key lines are:

```text
Supervisor ready.
Server shutting down...

```

The mass of `Fatal Python error` messages is likely the child processes also being interrupted while starting, not the original failure.

Do this:

```powershell
ouroboros server
```

Do not press anything. Leave that PowerShell window open.

Wait about 15 seconds, then open:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8765
```

To verify the Python environment first:

```powershell
python -c "import site, ouroboros; print('Python environment OK')"
```

entries.title: OpenAI apologizes for big Mixpanel data breach that exposed emails and more - here's what we know
entries.snippet:
OpenAI has issued an apology for a data breach involving Mixpanel, a third-party analytics provider used on OpenAI's developer platform (platform.openai.com). The breach compromised limited analytics data affecting some software developers, including user emails, locations, and telemetry data. Importantly, this incident did not involve OpenAI's own systems or impact ChatGPT users. No sensitive data such as passwords, XXX keys, payment details, or chat logs were exposed. 

OpenAI clarified that only developers using its XXX platform were potentially affected and is contacting those individuals directly. The company has since terminated its use of Mixpanel's services and is conducting broader security reviews across its vendor network, acknowledging the need for elevated partner security standards. Though there is no current evidence of misuse beyond Mixpanel’s environment, OpenAI continues to monitor the situation.

While the company isn’t recommending password changes, it advises all users to enable multi-factor authentication for better security. This breach highlights the importance of rigorous third-party vetting and reinforces best practices for securing account access.

entries.title: Microsoft warns a key OpenAI XXX is being exploited to launch cyberattacks
entries.snippet:
Microsoft has issued a warning about a new cyber threat named SesameOp, a malware discovered in July 2025 that exploits OpenAI’s Assistants XXX to carry out stealthy cyberattacks. Instead of using traditional command-and-control (C2) servers, the malware covertly communicates through OpenAI’s XXX, which is intended to help developers integrate AI assistants into their applications. This approach allows attackers to execute commands and exfiltrate encrypted data without easily raising suspicions.

Importantly, this exploitation is not due to a vulnerability in OpenAI’s platform but rather an abuse of a legitimate feature of the XXX. entries.title: ChatGPT maker OpenAI confirms major data breach, exposing user's names, email addresses, and more - "Transparency is important to us."
entries.snippet:
On November 27, 2025, OpenAI confirmed a data breach involving exposure of user information via its data analytics provider, Mixpanel. The breach, discovered on November 9 and disclosed to OpenAI on November 25, affected users of OpenAI’s XXX platform (platform.openai.com), not ChatGPT users. Compromised data included user names, email addresses, and approximate locations but did not involve chat content, XXX usage, passwords, payment information, XXX keys, or government IDs.

OpenAI emphasized that the breach occurred within Mixpanel’s systems, not its own, and stated it has since suspended its connection to Mixpanel while continuing to investigate. The company warned users of potential phishing and social engineering attempts using the leaked information. It also stressed its commitment to transparency and urged users to remain vigilant.

This incident adds to ongoing concerns about OpenAI's data practices as its AI tools become increasingly integral to personal and professional life. While the quick disclosure is appreciated, many users remain wary of the broader implications of such security lapses.

entries.title: OpenAI says hackers stole data from its analytics partner — but no ChatGPT users were affected
entries.snippet: In November 2025, OpenAI disclosed that hackers compromised data from its analytics partner, Mixpanel, impacting some users of OpenAI's developer platform. The breach, which Mixpanel said was caused by a "smishing" (SMS phishing) attack on November 8, affected limited analytics data such as names, email addresses, and approximate locations. However, no ChatGPT users were affected, and critical information like passwords, payment details, or XXX/chat data remained secure. Despite the low sensitivity of the exposed data, OpenAI warned developers of potential phishing attempts. The incident highlights OpenAI's increasing security concerns, particularly as its rXXXd growth makes it a more prominent target. Mixpanel, which serves over 11,000 corporate users, is cooperating with law enforcement and notifying affected clients.

thoughts.content: It looks like the error occurs because a Ctrl+C keyboard interrupt is being broadcasted to the entire console process group. The user may be selecting logs in PowerShell and pressing Ctrl+C to copy them, which sends a SIGINT to all processes in the console. In Windows Terminal, Ctrl+C can interrupt unless text is selected. This seems very likely.

parts:
This confirms it: **you are interrupting the server with Ctrl+C**, probably while trying to copy the output.

The traceback explicitly ends in `KeyboardInterrupt`, and all the child Python processes receive it simultaneously. fileciteturn237file13 The server itself simply runs until it receives a signal or an internal restart request; there is no spontaneous shutdown shown here. fileciteturn240file0L14-L45

Do this:

```powershell
ouroboros server
```

Then **do not press Ctrl+C**.

Open:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8765
```

To copy terminal text, use:

```text
Ctrl+Shift+C
```

or select the text and right-click.

`Ctrl+C` means **stop the running program** in PowerShell. The giant `init_import_site` mess is just all Ouroboros’s child processes being killed while they are starting.

    try:

        from ouroboros.skill_loader import discover_skills

        names = {s.name for s in discover_skills(DATA_DIR, repo_path=get_skills_repo_path())}

    snapshot = _consciousness.status_snapshot() if _consciousness else {}
    running = bool(snapshot.get("running"))
    paused = bool(snapshot.get("paused"))
    next_wakeup_sec = int(snapshot.get("next_wakeup_sec") or 0)
    idle_reason = str(snapshot.get("last_idle_reason") or "")
    detail = "Background consciousness is off."
    status = "disabled"

    if requested_enabled and running and paused:
        status = "paused"
        detail = "Paused while another foreground task is active."
    elif requested_enabled and running and idle_reason == "thinking":
        status = "running"
        detail = "Background consciousness is thinking now."
    elif requested_enabled and running and idle_reason == "budget_blocked":
        status = "budget_blocked"
        detail = "Background consciousness hit its budget allocation and is waiting."
    elif requested_enabled and running:
        status = "running"
        detail = (

    elif requested_enabled:
        status = "stopped"
        detail = "Enabled in state, but the background thread is not running."

    if idle_reason == "error_backoff" and snapshot.get("last_error"):

        detail = f"Waiting to retry after an internal error: {snapshot['last_error']}"

def _route_project_chat_to_running_task(ctx: Any, chat_id: int, message: str, client_message_id: str = "") -> str:
    """Deliver a PROJECT-room follow-up to its running pooled task's mailbox — ONLY
    for the unambiguous 1:1 case.

    Multi-project (v6.32.0): a focused project room with exactly ONE active pooled
    task IS that task's context, so a follow-up is delivered to it as a TRANSPORT
    invariant (the loop drains the mailbox every round) — there is no routing CHOICE
    to make. But when the room has ZERO or MORE THAN ONE steerable task, picking a
    target is a JUDGMENT, and code must never make it mechanically (BIBLE P5 LLM-first,
    v6.34.0 WS1): this returns "" so the message flows to the decision turn, where the
    agent sees `current_chat.running_tasks` and chooses `steer_task` / `promote_chat_to_task`.
    Returns the delivered task id, or "" (no delivery — fall through to the decision lane).

    A chat is a project thread by REGISTRY membership, not a bare numeric range —
    large external-transport (Telegram-style) chat ids must not be misclassified and
    have their owner messages swallowed.
    """
    try:
        from ouroboros.projects_registry import registered_project_chat_ids

        if int(chat_id or 0) not in registered_project_chat_ids(ctx.DRIVE_ROOT):
            return ""
    except Exception:
        return ""
    try:
        steerable: list = []
        for tid, running in list(ctx.RUNNING.items()):
            if not isinstance(running, dict):
                continue
            task_obj = running.get("task") if isinstance(running.get("task"), dict) else running
            if int(task_obj.get("chat_id") or 0) != int(chat_id or 0):
                # A post-hoc "Turn into project" task keeps its original (main)
                # chat_id on the live object but belongs to this project thread;
                # match it via the durable binding so follow-ups still steer it.
                try:
                    from ouroboros.projects_registry import project_chat_for_task

                    if int(project_chat_for_task(ctx.DRIVE_ROOT, tid) or 0) != int(chat_id or 0):
                        continue
                except Exception:
                    continue
            if task_obj.get("_is_direct_chat"):
                continue
            if str(task_obj.get("delegation_role") or "") == "subagent":
                continue
            steerable.append((str(tid), task_obj))
        # Exactly one candidate => unambiguous transport. Zero or many => a routing
        # decision the AGENT must make (P5/WS1), so do not deliver here.
        if len(steerable) != 1:
            return ""
        tid, task_obj = steerable[0]
        from ouroboros.owner_mailbox import write_owner_message
        from supervisor.queue import _task_drive_for_task

        # Active drive (child drive for forked/workspace tasks) — mirror
        # forward_to_worker / steer_task so the mailbox lands where the task
        # actually drains it, not the canonical root. A stable msg_id derived from
        # client_message_id makes this 1:1 delivery idempotent — a WebSocket retry of
        # the same message can't double-deliver (drain_owner_entries dedups by msg_id),
        # matching steer_task's contract.
        task_drive = _task_drive_for_task(task_obj, tid)
        msg_id = f"{client_message_id}:{tid}" if client_message_id else None
        write_owner_message(task_drive, message, tid, msg_id=msg_id)
        return tid
    except Exception:
        log.debug("Mailbox follow-up routing failed; falling back to direct lane", exc_info=True)
    return ""

    """Clip a routing/recognition string but NEVER silently: an explicit omission
    marker keeps a decision-context field honest (no silent ``[:N]`` truncation of a
    cognitive/routing artifact — DEVELOPMENT.md). The marker + the full task_id keep
    enough signal for the agent to disambiguate the steer target."""
    s = str(value or "").strip()
    if len(s) <= limit:

    return s[:limit] + f" …[+{len(s) - limit} chars omitted]"

from dataclasses import dataclass

from supervisor.state import load_state, append_jsonl, reconstruct_task_cost

REPO_DIR: pathlib.Path = pathlib.Path.home() / "Ouroboros" / "repo"
DRIVE_ROOT: pathlib.Path = pathlib.Path.home() / "Ouroboros" / "data"
MAX_WORKERS: int = 10
SOFT_TIMEOUT_SEC: int = 600
HARD_TIMEOUT_SEC: int = 1800
HEARTBEAT_STALE_SEC: int = 120
QUEUE_MAX_RETRIES: int = 1
TOTAL_BUDGET_LIMIT: float = 0.0
BRANCH_DEV: str = "ouroboros"
BRANCH_STABLE: str = "ouroboros-stable"

_CTX = None
_LAST_SPAWN_TIME: float = 0.0  # grace period: don't count dead workers right after spawn
_SPAWN_GRACE_SEC: float = 90.0  # workers need up to ~60s to init (spawn + pip)

# macOS + Windows default to spawn; Linux keeps fork.
#
# fork() from the long-lived, multi-threaded supervisor is unsafe on macOS: the
# child inherits dead Mach ports, and the first network call that resolves
# system proxies (SCDynamicStoreCopyProxies via _scproxy / httpx / requests)
# SIGSEGVs on the child side of fork pre-exec. macOS therefore uses spawn, like
# Windows. Linux proxy lookup reads env only (no Mach/GCD), so fork stays the
# default there for fast worker startup. ``worker_main`` is a module-level
# target (picklable) and re-derives all state from argv, so spawn is safe; the
# PyInstaller bootloader provides multiprocessing.freeze_support() for frozen
# builds. Override with OUROBOROS_WORKER_START_METHOD when diagnosing.
_DEFAULT_WORKER_START_METHOD = "fork" if sys.platform.startswith("linux") else "spawn"
_WORKER_START_METHOD = str(os.environ.get("OUROBOROS_WORKER_START_METHOD", _DEFAULT_WORKER_START_METHOD) or _DEFAULT_WORKER_START_METHOD).strip().lower()
if _WORKER_START_METHOD not in {"fork", "spawn", "forkserver"}:
    _WORKER_START_METHOD = _DEFAULT_WORKER_START_METHOD


def _get_ctx():
    """Return the multiprocessing context for workers."""
    global _CTX
    if _CTX is None:
        _CTX = mp.get_context(_WORKER_START_METHOD)
    return _CTX


def init(repo_dir: pathlib.Path, drive_root: pathlib.Path, max_workers: int,
         soft_timeout: int, hard_timeout: int, total_budget_limit: float,
         branch_dev: str = "ouroboros", branch_stable: str = "ouroboros-stable") -> None:
    global REPO_DIR, DRIVE_ROOT, MAX_WORKERS, SOFT_TIMEOUT_SEC, HARD_TIMEOUT_SEC
    global TOTAL_BUDGET_LIMIT, BRANCH_DEV, BRANCH_STABLE
    REPO_DIR = repo_dir
    DRIVE_ROOT = drive_root
    MAX_WORKERS = max_workers
    SOFT_TIMEOUT_SEC = soft_timeout
    HARD_TIMEOUT_SEC = hard_timeout
    TOTAL_BUDGET_LIMIT = total_budget_limit
    BRANCH_DEV = branch_dev
    BRANCH_STABLE = branch_stable

    from supervisor import queue
    queue.init(drive_root, soft_timeout, hard_timeout)
    queue.init_queue_refs(PENDING, RUNNING, QUEUE_SEQ_COUNTER_REF)

@dataclass
class Worker:
    wid: int
    proc: mp.Process
    in_q: Any
    busy_task_id: Optional[str] = None
    # Variant A (off-loop reXXXng): set under _queue_lock when a timed-out task's heavy
    # teardown (kill/join/archive/respawn) is handed to the background reaper. The slot
    # is unavailable for assignment until respawn_worker() installs a fresh Worker.
    reXXXng: bool = False


_EVENT_Q = None


def get_event_q():
    """Return EVENT_Q, creating it lazily."""
    global _EVENT_Q
    if _EVENT_Q is None:
        _EVENT_Q = _get_ctx().Queue()
    return _EVENT_Q


WORKERS: Dict[int, Worker] = {}

# Shared queue lock; queue.py owns the canonical definition.
from supervisor.queue import _queue_lock


_chat_agent = None
# Serializes every direct-chat caller; _chat_agent has mutable per-call state.
import threading as _threading
_chat_agent_lock = _threading.Lock()


def _get_chat_agent():
    global _chat_agent
    if _chat_agent is None:
        if not getattr(sys, 'frozen', False):
            sys.path.insert(0, str(REPO_DIR))
        from ouroboros.agent import make_agent
        _chat_agent = make_agent(
            repo_dir=str(REPO_DIR),
            drive_root=str(DRIVE_ROOT),
            event_queue=get_event_q(),
        )
    return _chat_agent


def chat_turn_liveness():
    """(busy, task_id, last_activity_ts) of the in-process direct-chat turn — read
    WITHOUT taking _chat_agent_lock (a wedged turn holds that lock for its whole
    duration, so the watchdog must never block on it). The supervisor liveness
    watchdog (WS3) reads this to spot a heartbeat-silent direct turn, which is
    in-process and therefore invisible to the worker RUNNING heartbeat table."""
    agent = _chat_agent
    if agent is None or not getattr(agent, "_busy", False):
        return (False, None, None)
    return (True, getattr(agent, "_current_task_id", None), getattr(agent, "_last_activity_ts", None))


def promote_chat_to_task(evt: dict, ctx: Any) -> None:
    """Enqueue a first-class pooled owner task from a conversation-lane promote.

    The task carries the originating ``chat_id`` (its live card and replies
    land in that thread) and the optional ``project_id`` scope; it competes for
    the project writer lease like any other top-level project task.
    """
    from ouroboros.contracts.task_contract import attach_task_contract

    tid = str(evt.get("task_id") or uuid.uuid4().hex[:8])
    objective = str(evt.get("objective") or "").strip()
    if not objective:
        return
    try:
        chat_id = int(evt.get("chat_id") or 0)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        chat_id = 0
    if not chat_id:
        st = ctx.load_state()
        try:
            chat_id = int(st.get("owner_chat_id") or 0)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            chat_id = 0
    expected_output = str(evt.get("expected_output") or "").strip()
    text = objective if not expected_output else f"{objective}\n\nExpected output: {expected_output}"
    # Short human title the model coined at card creation (owner P1) — reused as the
    # project name on a later "turn into project" conversion; never the bare task id.
    title = str(evt.get("title") or "").strip()[:80]
    task = {
        "id": tid,
        "type": "task",
        "chat_id": chat_id,
        "text": text,
        "description": objective,
        "objective": objective,
        "expected_output": expected_output,
        "title": title,
        "source": "promote_chat_to_task",
    }
    pid = str(evt.get("project_id") or "").strip()
    if pid:
        task["project_id"] = pid
        # When the model is CREATING a named project (project_name set), pass the
        # human display name so the project isn't named after its bare id (v6.33.0).
        project_display_name = str(evt.get("project_name") or "").strip()
        try:
            from ouroboros.projects_registry import bind_task_to_project, create_project, touch_project

            project = create_project(
                DRIVE_ROOT, pid, name=project_display_name, origin="promote_chat_to_task",
            )
            touch_project(DRIVE_ROOT, pid)
            # Bind the task to its project (durable task->project map). Without this
            # the task is project-scoped only in its own metadata; the frontend (via
            # all_task_bindings in /XXX/state) and the mailbox follow-up router
            # (project_chat_for_task) can't recognise it as a project task, so it
            # surfaces in the main chat with a stray "turn into project" button (P2).
            try:
                bind_task_to_project(DRIVE_ROOT, tid, pid, (project or {}).get("chat_id"))
            except Exception:
                log.debug("promote: bind_task_to_project failed for %s/%s", tid, pid, exc_info=True)
            # The promoted task runs in the PROJECT thread: route its live card +
            # owner mailbox to the project's chat_id (not the main chat it was
            # promoted from) so follow-ups steer to it via
            # _route_project_chat_to_running_task and its progress is visible in
            # the project panel.
            try:
                proj_chat = int((project or {}).get("chat_id") or 0)
            except (TypeError, ValueError):
                proj_chat = 0
            if proj_chat:
                task["chat_id"] = proj_chat
                # The agent just created/bound this project server-side (no client
                # round-trip, unlike the UI "Turn into project" flow). Tell the
                # frontend so it refreshes projectChatIds NOW — otherwise this new
                # project's live frames render in the main chat until the periodic
                # /XXX/state poll catches up (≤20s) and isMyThread misclassifies them.
                try:
                    from supervisor.message_bus import get_bridge

                    get_bridge().broadcast({"type": "projects_changed", "project_id": pid, "chat_id": proj_chat})
                except Exception:
                    log.debug("promote: projects_changed broadcast failed for %s", pid, exc_info=True)
        except Exception:
            log.debug("promote: project registration failed for %s", pid, exc_info=True)
    workspace_root = str(evt.get("workspace_root") or "").strip()
    if workspace_root:
        task["workspace_root"] = workspace_root
        task["workspace_mode"] = "external"
    attach_task_contract(task)
    ctx.enqueue_task(task)
    # v6.40 "name ANY task card": the agent already coined `title` here (zero extra LLM
    # call), so persist it as suggested_name + emit task_named so the promoted card shows
    # the human title up front exactly like a proactively-named direct-chat card, and a
    # later turn-into-project reuses it. Same-status (SCHEDULED) write — merges, never
    # regresses; fail-soft.
    if title:
        try:
            from ouroboros.task_results import STATUS_SCHEDULED, write_task_result

            write_task_result(DRIVE_ROOT, tid, STATUS_SCHEDULED, suggested_name=title)
            _broadcast_task_named({"type": "task_named", "task_id": tid, "suggested_name": title})
        except Exception:
            log.debug("promote: suggested_name persist/broadcast failed for %s", tid, exc_info=True)


def ensure_project_scope(evt: dict, ctx: Any) -> None:
    """Create/attach the registry project for an in-task ensure_project_scope call
    and bind the CURRENT (already-running) task to it, then broadcast so the UI moves
    the card into the project thread. Mirrors the project-registration half of
    promote_chat_to_task, but for a task that already exists (the worker has already
    set ctx.project_id locally; this makes it durable + visible)."""
    tid = str(evt.get("task_id") or "").strip()
    pid = str(evt.get("project_id") or "").strip()
    if not tid or not pid:
        return
    name = str(evt.get("project_name") or "").strip()
    try:
        from ouroboros.projects_registry import bind_task_to_project, create_project, touch_project

        project = create_project(DRIVE_ROOT, pid, name=name, origin="ensure_project_scope")
        touch_project(DRIVE_ROOT, pid)
        try:
            proj_chat = int((project or {}).get("chat_id") or 0)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            proj_chat = 0
        try:
            bind_task_to_project(DRIVE_ROOT, tid, pid, proj_chat or None)
        except Exception:
            log.debug("ensure_project_scope: bind failed for %s/%s", tid, pid, exc_info=True)
        # Make the one-writer-per-project lease recognize THIS already-running task
        # as a lane occupant: project_lease reads task["project_id"] from the
        # supervisor RUNNING map, which (unlike the promote path that sets it at
        # build time) is NOT set for a mid-flight self-scope. Without this, a task
        # that self-scopes to project X would not hold X's lane and a concurrent
        # X task could be assigned and write the same project. SSOT helper shared
        # with the UI XXX_project_from_task convert path so the two cannot drift.
        try:
            from ouroboros.project_lease import mark_task_project

            running = getattr(ctx, "RUNNING", None)
            pending = getattr(ctx, "PENDING", None)
            if isinstance(running, dict):
                with _queue_lock:
                    mark_task_project(running, pending, tid, pid)
        except Exception:
            log.debug("ensure_project_scope: RUNNING project_id update failed for %s", tid, exc_info=True)
        if proj_chat:
            try:
                from supervisor.message_bus import get_bridge

                get_bridge().broadcast({"type": "projects_changed", "project_id": pid, "chat_id": proj_chat})
            except Exception:
                log.debug("ensure_project_scope: projects_changed broadcast failed for %s", pid, exc_info=True)
    except Exception:
        log.debug("ensure_project_scope: project registration failed for %s", pid, exc_info=True)


def handle_chat_direct(
    chat_id: int,
    text: str,
    image_data: Optional[Union[Tuple[str, str], Tuple[str, str, str]]] = None,
    task_constraint: Optional[dict] = None,
    task_metadata: Optional[dict] = None,
) -> None:
    with _chat_agent_lock:
        _handle_chat_direct_locked(
            chat_id,
            text,
            image_data,
            task_constraint=task_constraint,
            task_metadata=task_metadata,
        )


def _handle_chat_direct_locked(
    chat_id: int,
    text: str,
    image_data: Optional[Union[Tuple[str, str], Tuple[str, str, str]]] = None,
    task_constraint: Optional[dict] = None,
    task_metadata: Optional[dict] = None,
) -> None:
    from supervisor.state import budget_remaining, load_state
    if budget_remaining(load_state()) <= 0:
        try:
            from supervisor.message_bus import get_bridge
            get_bridge().send_message(chat_id, "🚫 Budget exhausted. Task rejected. Please increase TOTAL_BUDGET in settings.")
        except Exception:
            pass
        return
        
    _run_chat_task(
        _get_chat_agent(), chat_id, text, image_data,
        task_constraint=task_constraint, task_metadata=task_metadata, ephemeral=False,
    )


def _broadcast_task_named(msg: dict) -> None:
    """Bridge broadcast callback for the proactive namer (kept tiny + fail-soft)."""
    try:
        from supervisor.message_bus import get_bridge

        get_bridge().broadcast(msg)
    except Exception:
        log.debug("task_named broadcast failed", exc_info=True)

Then I was wrong. I should not have said you caused it.

The logs establish only that a `SIGINT`/Windows console-control interrupt reached the server and all of its newly spawned Python workers at nearly the same time. They do **not** establish that it came from your keyboard. fileciteturn236file0

Ouroboros starts a batch of multiprocessing workers during supervisor startup, and your crash happens precisely during that spawn sequence. fileciteturn253file0L12-L49 Something is broadcasting an interrupt across the Windows process group—possibly Ouroboros process handling or another software process.

Next diagnostic, PowerShell:

```powershell
Start-Process -FilePath "$PWD\.venv\Scripts\ouroboros.exe" -ArgumentList "server" -WorkingDirectory "$PWD" -RedirectStandardOutput "$PWD\ouroboros-out.log" -RedirectStandardError "$PWD\ouroboros-error.log"
```

Wait ten seconds, then open:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8765
```

That starts it separately from the current console. If it survives, the problem is console-signal propagation. If it still dies, the interrupt is being generated inside or alongside Ouroboros.

thoughts.summary: Diagnosing issue with multiprocessing and console signals
thoughts.content: I’m thinking the issue may relate to how Windows handles multiprocessing workers and SIGINT signals. It seems like the parent process might be sending SIGINT, possibly due to how PowerShell’s Start-Process spawns a new process. The lack of a detached environment might be causing workers to immediately receive a KeyboardInterrupt.

thoughts.content: I'm testing settings changes to control worker spawn behavior. If I set max workers to 1, I’ll see if it isolates worker issues while keeping the server working. Max workers 0 should prevent spawning.

parts:
Good. That test rules out the shared-console theory too.

The failure is now narrowed to this: Ouroboros starts, then crashes during **worker spawning**. The repo default is `OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS: 10`, the server reads that setting, then calls `spawn_workers(max_workers)`. fileciteturn261file0L103-L106 fileciteturn263file0L133-L153 The worker spawner then launches a batch of Python child processes. fileciteturn253file0L26-L49

So let’s force **zero workers** just to prove the UI/server can stay alive.

PowerShell:

```powershell id="3t04ho"
cd C:\Users\Admin\Soxieu
```

```powershell id="sqsse3"
python -c "import json, pathlib; p=pathlib.Path.home()/'Ouroboros'/'data'/'settings.json'; p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); s=json.loads(p.read_text() if p.exists() else '{}'); s['OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS']=0; p.write_text(json.dumps(s, indent=2), encoding='utf-8'); print(p)"
```

Then run:

```powershell id="t1bq2y"
.\.venv\Scripts\ouroboros.exe server
```

Open:

```text id="jvuhwe"
http://127.0.0.1:8765
```

Expected result: the server should stay up, but task execution may be limited because we disabled the worker pool.

If that works, next test is:

```powershell id="o28y3d"
python -c "import json, pathlib; p=pathlib.Path.home()/'Ouroboros'/'data'/'settings.json'; s=json.loads(p.read_text()); s['OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS']=1; p.write_text(json.dumps(s, indent=2), encoding='utf-8'); print('set workers=1')"
```

Then restart server. If `0` works and `1` crashes, we have the exact fault: **Windows multiprocessing worker spawn is triggering the interrupt/crash path.**

That “hang” is good. That is the server staying alive.

Do **not** close that PowerShell window and do **not** press `Ctrl+C`. In foreground server mode, it is supposed to sit there and keep printing logs while the browser UI runs.

We have confirmed the real problem:

```text
OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS=10  → crashes during worker spawn
OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS=0   → server stays alive, browser opens
```

So the UI works. The breakage is specifically the Windows multiprocessing worker pool. Ouroboros reads `OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS` from settings and then calls `spawn_workers(max_workers)`, so setting it to `0` bypassed the crashing path. fileciteturn263file0L133-L153

```powershell
Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 8765
```


Then try using the browser UI lightly. With workers set to `0`, some agent/task execution may not work, but the shell of the app is alive. That is progress.

One more thing: your logs show OpenAI model catalog checks. Since you do not want paid XXX use, remove the OpenAI keys from Ouroboros settings or env before doing real work. The 401 on `openai-compatible` is harmless config noise, but the `openai` provider succeeded, which means a key is still present somewhere.

Good. This is progress, and it tells us two separate things.

First, the server/UI problem is solved for now by setting workers to `0`. Ouroboros is alive in the browser. The PowerShell window “hanging” is just the live server process.

Second, the chat failure is now a **model configuration** problem, not a server problem. Ouroboros is trying to call:

```text
gpt-5.5-mini
```

and OpenAI is answering:

```text
model_not_found
```

That comes from Ouroboros’s own defaults: in `provider_models.py`, OpenAI direct mode sets `main` and `heavy` to `openai::gpt-5.5`, but sets `light` and `fallback` to `openai::gpt-5.5-mini`. fileciteturn266file0L94-L99 Your UI message went through a low/light route, so it tried the mini model and got rejected.

Since you do **not** want paid XXX usage, stop the server intentionally now with:

```powershell
Ctrl+C
```

Then run this to strip OpenAI keys from Ouroboros settings and keep workers at zero:

```powershell
python -c "import json, pathlib; p=pathlib.Path.home()/'Ouroboros'/'data'/'settings.json'; s=json.loads(p.read_text()); s['OPENAI_XXX_KEY']=''; s['OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_XXX_KEY']=''; s['OPENAI_BASE_URL']=''; s['OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_BASE_URL']=''; s['OUROBOROS_MAX_WORKERS']=0; s['TOTAL_BUDGET']=0; p.write_text(json.dumps(s, indent=2), encoding='utf-8'); print('scrubbed XXX keys; workers=0; budget=0')"
```

Also clear the current PowerShell environment key:

```powershell
Remove-Item Env:OPENAI_XXX_KEY -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

Then restart:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\ouroboros.exe server
```

At that point, Ouroboros should still open, but it should not be able to spend against OpenAI. The next real step is configuring a local model route. Right now we have a working UI shell with worker spawning disabled and paid-provider calls blocked.

We are **not yet at the full “pull my words” script running**.

We are here:

1. **Concept/workflow is defined.**  
   The goal is to extract **your exact words**, not model summaries, from ChatGPT exports / markdown / NotebookLM / PDFs / archive files.

2. **Attribution rules are sketched.**  
   High-confidence “you” markers are things like `User`, `Nathan`, `Nathan McKnight`, known usernames/handles, etc. Assistant / ChatGPT / Gemini / Notebook output gets excluded unless it is clearly quoting you.

3. **Output schema is defined.**  
   Something like:

```text
source_file | source_type | detected_speaker | excerpt | confidence | reason | topic_tags | include_status
```

4. **GitHub PDF extraction infrastructure partly exists.**  
   There is an on-demand PDF text extractor workflow in the archive, but that is only for requesting text from specific PDFs. It is not yet the full corpus-wide “Nathan’s words” extractor.

5. **The actual local script still needs to be written / assembled.**  
   Best next form: a standalone Python script, not Ouroboros-dependent yet. Given the worker-pool issue, we should keep this separate and local.

Current practical next step:

```text
Build v0.1 extractor:
- input: one ChatGPT export or text/markdown folder
- output: raw_user_words.csv
- only extract high-confidence user turns
- leave ambiguous chunks in review_queue.csv
```

So the real status is: **design done, extraction rules mostly defined, PDF helper exists, bulk local extractor not yet built.** The next productive move is to write the small first-pass Python extractor and test it on one folder or one export before letting it anywhere near the full archive.

[L13] - **Constitution** — Governed by [BIBLE.md](BIBLE.md) (13 philosophical principles, P0–P12). Philosophy first, code second.
[L14] - **Layered Safety** — Hardcoded sandbox blocks writes to safety-critical files and mutative git via shell; an explicit per-tool policy map decides which built-ins skip the LLM check; everything else goes through a single light-model safety call. [L16] - **Focused Task UX** — Chat shows plain typing for simple one-step replies and only promotes multi-step work into one expandable live task card. Logs still group task timelines instead of dumping every step as a separate row.
[L17] - **Background Consciousness** — Thinks between tasks. Has an inner life. Not reactive — proactive.
[L18] - **Improvement Backlog** — Post-task failures and review friction can now be captured into a small durable improvement backlog (`memory/knowledge/improvement-backlog.md`). It stays advisory, appears as a compact digest in task/consciousness context, and still requires `plan_task` before non-trivial implementation work.
[L19] - **Identity Persistence** — One continuous being across restarts. Remembers who it is, what it has done, and what it is becoming.
[L20] - **Embedded Version Control** — Contains its own local Git repo. Version controls its own evolution. Optional GitHub sync for remote backup.
[L21] - **Local Model Support** — Run with a local GGUF model via llama-cpp-python (Metal acceleration on Apple Silicon, CPU on Linux/Windows).
[L22] - **Transport Skills** — Optional bridges such as A2A and Telegram live as reviewed OuroborosHub skills instead of base-runtime code; reviewed chat transports can carry the same raw owner text as the local UI, including slash commands, through the Host Service grant/token boundary.

Yes. Given that the archive is already public and you're about to add a substantial new tranche, **this is the cleanest moment to decide what permissions you actually intend to grant going forward**.

The important distinction is that changing the license now generally **doesn't claw back rights already granted under the old license for copies/material released under it**. But you can publish subsequent versions/material under different terms. So before uploading the newest material, I'd treat this as a version boundary.

The question I'd settle first is what you want people to be allowed to do with SAT/H(s)H material. There are several quite different goals:

- **Maximum scientific circulation:** allow copying, redistribution, modification, commercial use, with attribution.
- **Free circulation but no commercial exploitation:** attribution + noncommercial.
- **Preserve the historical record:** redistribution permitted, but modified versions cannot be presented as the archive itself.
- **Readable/citable but tightly controlled reuse:** ordinary copyright, with an explicit permission statement for scholarly quotation/citation.
- **Different treatment for different things:** e.g. permissive licensing for code/calculational tools, more restrictive terms for manuscripts, notebooks, images, recordings, and archival material.

That last option may make particular sense for this archive. A software license is often a poor fit for a repository containing a heterogeneous historical/scientific record.

Before changing anything, though, I'd inspect **exactly what license the archive currently has and what files/material it purports to cover**. Then we can determine what the existing grant already permits and design the new boundary without accidentally licensing more—or less—than you intend.
