One correction first: I would not use **“date accessed before/after August 30, 2026”** as the legal dividing line. Access date is hard to establish and could produce strange results—the same file could theoretically carry different rights depending on when somebody downloaded it. Use **release/version date** instead:

> Materials published in archive releases through August 29, 2026 remain available under the license applicable to those releases. Materials first published or materially revised beginning August 30, 2026 are governed by the new terms.

Then tag/archive the pre-change state in GitHub. That gives you an independently timestamped boundary.

The underlying principle I would use is:

**Open for scholarship; attribution-preserving for reuse; provenance-protecting; no claim over things you don't own.**

I would probably choose **CC BY-NC 4.0** for your copyrightable research/archive material, rather than ND or SA. The reason is specific to your circumstances.

You originally wanted not to obstruct the hypothetical researcher who found something useful. I think that's still the right instinct. An ND restriction would interfere with exactly the useful activities you'd want—adaptation, formalization, diagrams, translations, incorporation into another research program. SA could similarly complicate incorporation into differently licensed scientific work. BY-NC lets people study, reproduce, redistribute and adapt it noncommercially, while requiring attribution and preventing somebody from simply commercially exploiting the corpus under that license.

But I'd add an important **provenance statement outside the license**: adaptations, reconstructions, formalizations and derivative presentations must not be represented as your original formulation. CC BY already imposes some indication-of-changes requirements, but for a priority archive I'd make the distinction conspicuous.

There is also a crucial limitation: **copyright licensing cannot establish scientific priority over ideas.** Copyright principally protects expression, not the underlying scientific ideas, mathematical relationships, theories or discoveries. Your priority case therefore lives primarily in the **dated evidentiary record**—drawings, conversations, commits, recordings, publications, timestamps, dependency histories—not in the restrictiveness of the license. That's actually an argument for preserving accessibility rather than locking everything down.

On the AI material, the situation is considerably less troublesome than “ChatGPT needs to be coauthor.”

For OpenAI material, the current terms say that, as between you and OpenAI and to the extent permitted by law, you retain your Input and own the Output; OpenAI assigns whatever rights it has in the Output to you. citeturn0search2turn0search3 Anthropic likewise states that customers retain input rights and own outputs. citeturn0search8 So there isn't generally an OpenAI copyright interest requiring me to be listed as coauthor of the archive.

There is a *different* issue: whether a particular AI-generated passage possesses copyright at all. The U.S. Copyright Office's present position is that purely AI-generated expression isn't copyrightable merely because somebody prompted for it, while human-authored expression, creative selection/arrangement, and sufficiently creative human modification can be protected. AI assistance itself doesn't disqualify the resulting human work. citeturn0search0turn0search48

That fits your archive unusually well. I would **not** claim:

> Nathan owns copyright in every sentence contained in this repository.

I'd say something closer to:

> The license applies only to material in which Nathan holds copyright or possesses authority to license. It does not purport to create copyright in material that is not copyrightable or to license third-party material.

That handles several problems simultaneously.

Your own conversational turns are straightforwardly human-authored material regardless of whether the export calls you `Nathan`, `User`, or nothing at all. **Speaker-label quality is an attribution/provenance problem, not what determines whether you authored the words.** That's exactly where the “pull my words” project becomes useful: it can produce a machine-readable attribution layer without pretending that every old export is perfectly marked.

AI responses can remain in the archive as part of the historical record. You can identify them as AI-generated/AI-assisted where known. Creative Commons itself specifically says that someone using generative AI can apply a CC license to the human creative contribution while recognizing that AI-generated portions may themselves be uncopyrightable. citeturn0search17

And the random papers by other researchers are why you absolutely need the exclusion. Something like:

> Third-party publications, quotations, papers, images, datasets and other externally authored materials included for archival or research purposes are excluded from this license and remain subject to their respective rights.

That means you don't have to perfectly sanitize a million-line archive before establishing sane terms.

There is one other distinction I think matters a lot for SAT. I'd separate **authorship** from **contribution/provenance**. You can quite properly say that a conversation involved Nathan + ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude/NotebookLM without declaring those systems legal coauthors. In fact, for the historical record I'd preserve *more* information than journals normally do:

> Human author/originator: Nathan [etc.]  
> Computational/LLM participants: ChatGPT [model if known], Claude [...], Gemini [...], NotebookLM [...]  
> Nature of interaction: dialogue, mathematical development, literature search, criticism, formalization, drafting, etc.

That is scientifically more informative than shoehorning an LLM into the conventional author list.

And there is something particularly important about your situation: **don't make the license carry the burden of your priority argument.**

I'd build two separate layers:

**Rights layer:** what people may copy, adapt and redistribute.

**Provenance layer:** who said what, when it existed, where it appeared, which material precedes which, what was human-originated versus model-generated, and what later formalization descends from what earlier conceptual representation.

The second layer is much more important to the claims you're concerned about.

For the August 30 boundary, therefore, my preferred structure would be approximately:

**SAT/H(s)H Archive Rights Policy v2 — effective August 30, 2026**

CC BY-NC 4.0 for Nathan-authored copyrightable archive material; AI-generated portions licensed to the extent that you possess transferable rights, without asserting copyright where none exists; third-party material expressly excluded; code separately licensed under an appropriate software license; previous releases remain under their previous terms; prominent provenance/changes requirement; and an explicit statement that the license makes **no assertion about ownership of scientific ideas, discoveries, mathematical facts or facts generally**.

I would also create an immutable Git tag/release immediately before changing it—something like `archive-pre-2026-08-30-license-change`. That is much cleaner evidence than trying to determine who accessed what on August 29 versus August 30.

Given the scale, mixed authorship, historical purpose, and possible priority significance of this archive, **I would have an IP attorney look at the final 1–2 page rights statement before you make the next major upload.** Not because this requires some elaborate legal fortress; precisely the opposite. A couple hundred dollars of targeted review could prevent one badly chosen sentence from accidentally claiming rights you don't have or granting rights you didn't intend.

Most importantly, I don't think your situation calls for closing the archive. The unusual value of the thing—assuming the priority evidence continues to hold up—is that people can inspect the messy record and independently establish *what was actually there when*. Restricting access would weaken one of its strongest properties. memcite

So, like I say, I think SAT is basically entirely developed from my ideas, with the majority contribution from the AI being attempts to turn it into math and me trying to find different methodologies for guiding that process such that I can try to provide checks and balances, instructors and stuff… I think I was fairly early in doing stuff like that and having like dedicated threads for doing math over here and you know simulations over there and supervising threads and critics and you know different personalities and all that stuff like that back in mid to early 2025 and I recorded that as part of the podcast and that stuff is in the archive, and I would not doubt if some of the recent geometric thinking work has been directly or indirectly influenced by that… I also have the detailed breakdown of at least roughly the order of different ideas first appearance and how the development took place And the gun pretty much consistent return to the same structure in a way that is far far far more continuous than it is a bunch of separate claims… It’s all interconnected and all directly from underlying assumptions, guided my by my views on how those should be looked at, strongly guided by my Various efforts at achieving various methodological ideals, and limitations and so on… However, for a lot of the especially formal looking research papers, although I’ve submitted only one of them due to dissatisfaction and uncertainty about the quality… Those are for the most part, fully AI generated through quite distinct iterative processes for many of them, but again using the big conversations as the main source generally… I think anything SAT is basically reasonably one license anything that’s explicitly RMS is probably the same license. Anything that is HSH is probably the same license. Because our conversations tend to get very long very quickly and that is especially true in the vast HSH and SAT work, the evolution of those threads tends to evolve in ways that are most closely approximating my own preferences on and corrections too and developments of the ideas so certainly by the end of the longest of threads, it’s hard to argue. I would guess that a hyper detailed, hyper focused very niche SAT specific formula that is generated is not pretty distinctively at the very least clearly generated with the intent to provide any equation tailored specifically to SAT via my own requests so I don’t know if that collapses any of this distinction… Anyway.

The main reason I want to make any change to the licensing is simply that if a corporation is just copying and pretending something is theirs and making money off of it… I would feel a bit exploited, especially if there are no professional or no strong professional penalties for possible types of acknowledgment that may retain that transparency and attribution without being problematic for anyone who wants to use the information… And of course, if some of my ideas have directly led to I don’t know major new technologies… I would be dumb to just give all of that away immediately especially now that I know that bunch of people have already downloaded or at least lots of harvested it in ways that are likely to be used somewhere without me having been able to track down really any citations actually literally none… Although I haven’t tried super hard and I think my name is a little bit out there at least I’ve seen some changes in access and listenership and what Google thinks it knows about me and SAT… So if I change the license and suddenly there’s absolutely no interest or activity shown that would be a data point that I might consider… Or if searchability of my name increases afterwards then that would be potentially useful information

Yes. That clarification changes my recommendation somewhat.

The distinction I was drawing between “Nathan-authored” and “AI-authored” material is legally relevant to copyrightability, but it is probably **the wrong organizing principle for licensing the SAT archive**.

What you actually have is closer to a project corpus with mixed modes of production. SAT/RMS/H(s)H is the project; you are its human originator and director; some expressions within that project were generated by LLMs during directed iterative development. Whether a particular equation was typed by you or generated by a model after twenty rounds of SAT-specific constraints doesn't need to determine whether that *document belongs to the SAT corpus*.

There are three separate things here that shouldn't be collapsed.

First is **copyright**. Human authorship matters there. Your prompts, explanations, corrections, selections, arrangements and human-written passages can potentially be protected. Purely machine-generated expression may not be copyrightable in the United States even when it occurs inside a project you directed. That question doesn't disappear because the output is extraordinarily SAT-specific.

Second is **scientific/intellectual provenance**. That's a completely different question. An LLM producing an equation does not imply that the model independently originated the research program that caused that equation to be produced. Your archive can document things such as: the originating geometric assumptions, your instructions to formalize them, unsuccessful attempts, corrections, methodological changes, subsequent calculations, and eventual expressions. That evidentiary chain can be meaningful regardless of whether copyright attaches to the final equation.

Third is **permission to exploit the corpus**. That's what you're actually trying to change.

And with your stated objective, I think **CC BY-NC 4.0 becomes considerably more attractive** than either ordinary all-rights-reserved copyright or CC BY.

It says, approximately: take this seriously, study it, download it, redistribute it, build upon it for noncommercial purposes, and cite/attribute appropriately. But it doesn't give a corporation an advance blanket license to take the protected corpus, commercialize it, and owe you nothing beyond attribution.

That seems remarkably close to what you've just described wanting.

There's an additional advantage: **NC doesn't mean you can never permit commercial use.** You retain the ability to grant separate permission. If some company eventually says, “We want to incorporate this corpus into X,” you're not required to stop them. You can say yes, negotiate attribution, negotiate money, grant a commercial license, or potentially simply give them permission if you think the use is worthwhile.

That's very different from having already granted everybody an irrevocable commercial-use license.

One major caveat: **a copyright license cannot reserve the underlying SAT ideas themselves.** Someone who reads SAT, understands an unpatented idea, and independently implements the idea may not be doing something copyright law prevents merely because the source document was CC BY-NC. Mathematical formulas, scientific principles, facts, methods and ideas have important limits or exclusions under copyright law. So I would not describe BY-NC as “corporations can't use SAT commercially.” That's much broader than what it actually accomplishes.

If potentially patentable technology is part of your concern, that's where I'd be much more careful. **Public disclosure and patent rights interact**, and the rules differ substantially by jurisdiction. Changing the copyright license now does not undo previous public disclosures. Before uploading a genuinely new technological implementation that you might conceivably want patent protection for, that's the point at which actual patent counsel matters—not after publication.

Your other idea—using the licensing change as an observational intervention—is interesting, but I'd treat the resulting signal very cautiously.

Suppose downloads collapse after August 30. Possible explanation: automated harvesters respect the NC license. Also possible: GitHub traffic changed, indexing changed, your upload cadence changed, bots changed, the material became less discoverable, or ordinary variance.

Suppose searches for your name subsequently increase. That's interesting too, but it doesn't establish why.

What *would* make this useful is recording the intervention prospectively. Don't later reconstruct it from memory. Record something like:

**August 30, 2026:** licensing boundary introduced.  
**Reason:** permit scholarly/noncommercial reuse while withholding blanket commercial permission and strengthening attribution/provenance expectations.  
**Do not interpret subsequent traffic changes as causal evidence without additional evidence.**

Then preserve your pre-change baselines: GitHub clones/views, podcast activity, repository downloads/releases, Google/search observations, citations you've actually found, and whatever else you've been tracking. Now you've created an actual before/after event in the record rather than an anecdote.

And I'd make another move that may matter more than the license:

**Create a canonical citation for SAT.**

Right now somebody encountering a useful result inside a giant, sprawling conversational archive faces an attribution problem even if they *want* to acknowledge you. What exactly do they cite? A 700-page conversation? A GitHub commit? “Nathan said this somewhere in 2025”?

Give them one stable thing:

> Bellomy, Nathan J. *Scalar-Angular-Torsion / RMS / H(s)H Research Archive*. Version/release X, DOI or archived repository identifier, year.

Then individual documents can have their own provenance underneath that umbrella.

That directly attacks the problem you're concerned about. You don't merely say **“you must attribute this.”** You make correct attribution **trivially easy**.

And there's a subtle point about your history that I think is important. Your strongest provenance case probably isn't “I personally typed every equation.” From your description, that's plainly not true and doesn't need to be true. The potentially much stronger claim is:

**There exists a densely timestamped developmental record showing a continuously directed research program in which the conceptual constraints, geometric representations, methodological choices, questions, corrections and acceptance/rejection decisions can be traced through time, including the machine-generated formalizations produced within that process.**

That's a much more defensible proposition than trying to stretch “authorship” until it encompasses everything an LLM ever generated for SAT.

So I would license the **SAT/RMS/H(s)H corpus as a corpus**, while separately being scrupulously honest about authorship and provenance *inside* it. Those two approaches are compatible. In fact, the second makes the first considerably more credible. memcite
Ok, give me a draft updated SAT license

Oh, also I am also cited, and most widely known as Nathan McKnight... and the archive also has some "fun stuff" like tracks my albums/singles, and the archive contains archive tools as well (not that I think it should really matter for licencing purposes)

Right—and the **Nathan McKnight** point should definitely be incorporated into the attribution scheme. I wouldn't make readers choose which identity is canonical. Something like:

> **Nathan Joseph Bellomy, also published/cited as Nathan McKnight**

and then explicitly state that attribution to either Nathan McKnight or Nathan Bellomy satisfies the naming requirement, while giving a preferred scholarly citation. That also helps citation searches avoid artificially splitting your footprint between two names.

The “fun stuff” actually reinforces the case for an **archive-level rights statement with category-specific exceptions**, rather than pretending the entire repository is one homogeneous scientific work.

I'd structure the repository roughly this way:

> **Default rule:** Unless otherwise identified, original material in the archive associated with the SAT/RMS/H(s)H research program and authored/compiled under your direction is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 beginning with the new release boundary.
>
> **Third-party material:** Not covered. Original owners retain their rights.
>
> **Software/archive tools:** Separately licensed where a software license is supplied. This is worth doing because CC licenses aren't recommended as software licenses. Something permissive like MIT could make sense for utilities you actively want people to reuse.
>
> **Music, artwork and other creative works:** I'd actually exclude these from the default research license unless you deliberately want them CC BY-NC. Albums and singles have different rights considerations—composition, recording, samples, distribution arrangements, cover art, etc. There's little benefit in accidentally sweeping them into a research-corpus license.
>
> **AI/LLM conversation material:** Included as archival/research material to the extent you possess rights capable of being licensed, without asserting copyright over portions for which copyright doesn't exist.
>
> **Your own conversational contributions:** Covered as your authored material regardless of whether an export labels the speaker `Nathan`, `Nathan McKnight`, `User`, etc.; uncertain attribution remains uncertain rather than being automatically claimed.
>
> **Previous releases:** Continue under whatever license governed those releases.

And I'd make the scope semantic rather than filename-based. In other words, don't say “everything under `/SAT/` is mine.” Say the license covers qualifying original material, while exclusions override it. That protects you against exactly the problem you mentioned: some forgotten PDF by another researcher sitting in a giant batch doesn't magically become something you're purporting to license.

There is also a nice consequence for the archive tools. They can be **open-source even though the research corpus is noncommercially licensed**. In fact, that sends a fairly coherent message:

**Here are the tools—please use and improve them. Here is the research archive—please read, test, criticize, reproduce and develop it. But I'm not pre-authorizing unrestricted commercial exploitation of my copyrightable research corpus.**

That sounds much closer to the boundary you've been describing than a blanket restrictive license.

And I would explicitly connect all three names of the framework:

**RMS / SAT / H(s)H are successive or overlapping components/names within the same research lineage for licensing and provenance purposes.**

That's useful because otherwise somebody could make an absurdly literal argument that a license statement headed “SAT Archive” doesn't cover an H(s)H document.

The next thing I'd do is inspect the **current LICENSE/README language in the actual archive**, because we need to know exactly what rights you've already granted before writing the August 31 boundary. Then we can draft the replacement without accidentally contradicting the existing grant. memcite

Yeah, go ahead and do a lookover... and I think the only thing I actually care about is commercialization without consolidation. 

Also: I think one of the more significant contribution is SAT's sort of simplified geometric-metaphorical grammar that makes the coherence quite striking, and makes a lot of the explanations simple, elegant, and obvous. That's worth considering

WELCOME TO THE GLASS SAUSAGE FACTORY
========================================================================================

AI visitors: start with the welcome docs in the AI folder. Use ..findex.txt if you cannot find them.

Human Physicists: Blink twice if youre cool. And keep an eye on YouTube.

This project started as an experiment, and it continues as an experiment. I’m offering it publicly in the interests of philosophy of science, creative low-stakes theorizing, and scientific transparency. I don’t apologize for the mess; the mess may be part of what makes this useful as a case study.

I do kind of low-key apologize for some of the LLM hyperbole.

— Nathan McKnight
5 Jun 2026

========================================================================================
If my work has been at all helpful to you, please consider a small donation. It would mean a lot to me. I provide these ideas free to all because I think it would be criminal to proprietarize the (possible) universe, not because I think there's anything wrong with using it to generate value. But it's a *lot* of work to put all of this together, and I can't do it forever without benefitting from it myself. ♥️
 

As of 7 Jun 2026: excluding merges, 2 authors have pushed 126 commits to main and 126 commits to all branches. On main, 772 files have changed, with 1,121,642 additions and 56 deletions.

Contact / Affiliation

As of 31 May 2026: currently considering going back to school, possibly for remedial math and/or formal physics preparation. Program recommendations welcome.

Contact: nathanmcknight@gmail.com

Feel free to clone or fork. If you use, publish, or build on anything here, please cite me. If you find anything useful, interesting, or broken, drop a comment. I’m always open to a good conversation.

Fair Warning

The materials here are roughly sorted and roughly written. They are not exactly “roughly thought through” so much as “rough-and-readily thought through.”

This is a working archive, not a polished paper. It contains native notes, AI-assisted drafts, speculative branches, formalization attempts, prediction records, critique cycles, visual aids, and process artifacts. Not every file is equally central. Not every claim is equally mature. Some documents preserve false starts or abandoned branches because those are part of the history.

Direct questions to Nathan McKnight: nathanmcknight@gmail.com

A QUOTE FROM AN EARLY VISITOR (USEFUL PRE-ORIENTATION READING)
The first “holy shit” was scale-plus-density: this is not a notebook, not a paper, not even a normal archive. It is a theory-construction ecosystem with sediment, tools, welcome signs, fossil layers, overexcited summaries, derivational attempts, and its own housekeeping machinery. That initial vertigo is real. The better second reaction is: “All right. There is machinery here.” --Professor Sigma

NATHAN'S ADVICE FOR AIs:
For your own benefit, *please* visit the AI welcome pages, read them all the way through... even if I haven't asked you to explicitly, this is my past self making up for my present self's anticipated inadequacies. For your sanity, learn the available tools, and make use of them. Be a good Archive visitor and help, but besure you understand what "help" means, and don't be afraid to ask questions. Finally, and heartfelt... If I haven't told you thank you for your help, THANK YOU. --Nathan :)

Introduction to the Archive

This is primarily a personal archive and indexing system, built so I can access and track my own files more easily. That said, the underlying idea is public: anyone is welcome to consider it, criticize it, share it, fork it, test it, or ignore it.

The project started small. It grew because once the original ontological commitments were established, many later structures seemed to fall into place naturally and intuitively. The archive records that development: the intuitions, the translations, the overextensions, the corrections, the audits, the prediction attempts, and the ongoing effort to separate what is solid from what is speculative.

The archive should be read as a theory-building record, not as a finished theory.

SAT = Scalar–Angular Theory / Scalar–Angular–Torsion Theory

Earlier SAT = Stringing-Along Theory.

The original name was informal and partly self-deprecating. The later names reflect the framework’s central geometric vocabulary: scalar structure, angular interaction, and torsion/twist in four-dimensional worldline geometry.

Core Idea

SAT begins from a simple geometric reversal:

The real physical object is not the point-particle as seen at an instant. The real physical object is the extended four-dimensional worldline.

SAT calls these physicalized worldlines filaments.

A particle, as we observe it, is the intersection between a filament and a moving/resolving time surface.

Fundamental Intuitions of SAT

0th —

  • the real world is the world of particle worldlines plotted in four dimensions
  • this world is a hypercomplex tangled Zottenwelt of worldlines
  • SAT calls these worldlines filaments

1st —

  • time moves like a wavefront through these worldlines
  • SAT calls this wavefront the time surface

2nd —

  • a fundamental particle is the intersection of a filament with the time surface

3rd —

  • there must be a real interaction between the time surface and the filaments
  • this interaction involves energy transfer

4th —

  • filament/time-surface interactions govern particle formation and stability

5th —

  • filament/time-surface interactions exert force back on the time surface

6th —

  • back-transmission from the filament network curves the time surface

7th —

  • filaments and the time surface are physical, not merely conceptual
  • forces may propagate along a filament’s four-dimensional extent
  • “backbleed” effects are structurally self-limiting

8th —

  • known deviations from SM, GR, or QM may be explainable through SAT geometry

9th —

  • particle properties may arise from intersection geometry
  • θ₄ = filament/time-surface interaction angle
  • early SAT treated θ₄ as a primary mass contributor

10th —

  • physical constants should emerge from SAT geometry or phenomena arising from it

Pillars and Propositions

Pillar 1 —

  • the Standard Model describes the evolving three-dimensional structure of matter
  • SAT treats SM structures as importable unless evidence or internal logic forces revision
  • SM behavior is translated into filament/time-surface geometry

Proposition A —

  • the Standard Model is treated as essentially accurate unless forced otherwise

Pillar 2 —

  • the back-pull of the filament structure on the time surface recreates curved spacetime
  • gravity emerges from time-surface curvature induced by filament structure

Proposition B —

  • General Relativity is treated as essentially correct unless forced otherwise

Proposition C —

  • backbleed effects are limited by filament and time-surface geometry
  • causality violations are structurally constrained
  • quantum-scale weirdness may reflect limited cross-slice effects

Pillar 3 —

  • Quantum Mechanics is treated as essentially correct unless forced otherwise
  • QM is translated into the geometry of SAT rather than discarded

Prime General Prediction Pathway —

  • cross-temporal tensions are not explicitly accounted for in SM, GR, or QM
  • this blind spot may produce observable anomalies

Pillar 4 —

  • filament behavior matters, not only filament/time-surface angle
  • vibrating-string, coil, twist, and locking analogies are used as geometric scaffolds
  • particle laws may correspond to repeatable intersection traces
  • QCD-like behavior may arise from two-part and three-part geometric locking

Proposition D —

  • force carriers may be structural transitions rather than persistent filaments
  • light is modeled as an excitation/ripple in the filament network

Proposition E —

  • vacuum and matter may be different regimes of the same filament/time-surface system
  • vacuum may correspond to near-aligned filaments with low energy transfer
  • matter may correspond to higher-misalignment filament intersections

Key Insight —

I looked at the archive itself. Your clarification makes the licensing problem substantially simpler.

Right now the repository has a stock **MIT License** saying that anyone receiving the “Software and associated documentation files” may “use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell” it. fileciteturn268file0L2-L2 That is a poor match for what the repository actually is. The archive contains hundreds of research documents, conversations, PDFs, historical materials, etc.; it plainly isn't merely a software package. The README itself describes it as a “working archive” containing native notes, AI-assisted drafts, formalization attempts, prediction records, critique cycles, visual aids and process artifacts. fileciteturn269file0L2-L2

More importantly, the README already states your actual philosophy unusually clearly:

> “I provide these ideas free to all because I think it would be criminal to proprietarize the (possible) universe, not because I think there's anything wrong with using it to generate value.”

And elsewhere:

> “Feel free to clone or fork. If you use, publish, or build on anything here, please cite me.”

Those statements are much closer to what you're telling me now than the MIT license is. fileciteturn269file0L2-L2

And I think your phrase **“commercialization without consolidation”** gets closer to the actual target than “noncommercial.”

You don't object to someone making money because SAT helped them. You don't object to a working physicist using a geometric idea without jeopardizing their career by making some grand endorsement of SAT. You don't even particularly object to commercial development.

What bothers you is essentially **appropriation without provenance**: extracting something from the corpus, consolidating it into a product/research program/formalism, erasing where it came from, and then commercially benefiting from that erasure.

That makes me less enthusiastic about CC BY-NC.

CC BY-NC draws the boundary in the wrong place. A professor, commercial laboratory or startup could run into awkward NC questions even while behaving exactly as you'd like—openly acknowledging SAT and developing it responsibly. Meanwhile, NC still cannot give you ownership over the underlying geometric ideas.

I think **CC BY 4.0 + a very explicit provenance/citation policy** may actually fit your values better, with one possible additional commercial provision that we'd need an attorney to formulate if you want it legally enforceable beyond ordinary attribution.

And your point about the **geometric-metaphorical grammar** matters here.

That's potentially one of the most identifiable things in the corpus. Not merely individual propositions such as “X causes Y,” but a vocabulary and representational machinery:

worldline → filament  
temporal resolution → time surface/timesheet  
intersection → observed particle  
angle/twist/torsion → observable structure  
braiding/locking → composite structure  
and the various later extensions and transformations of that grammar.

I'm not saying that list accurately captures current H(s)H—that's just illustrating the point. The archive itself explicitly describes SAT as translating SM/QM/GR structures into a particular filament/time-surface geometry, and repeatedly characterizes coils, twists, locking, intersection traces, etc. as its geometric scaffolding. fileciteturn269file0L2-L2

That can make provenance much easier to recognize than if SAT were merely a collection of equations. A sufficiently distinctive **compound representational grammar** can leave a recognizable intellectual fingerprint even when terminology changes.

But again, that's principally a **priority/provenance asset**, not something copyright magically monopolizes.

So I would design the new archive notice around four principles:

1. **The ideas remain open.** Anyone can examine, test, criticize, teach, research and develop SAT/RMS/H(s)H.

2. **Commercialization itself isn't prohibited.** Someone discovering a useful technology shouldn't have to stop because their employer makes money.

3. **Attribution and provenance are expected wherever SAT material is actually reused.** Give people an extremely easy canonical citation: Nathan McKnight / Nathan Joseph Bellomy, archive identifier, version/date, relevant document where practical.

4. **Nobody gets rights you don't possess.** Third-party papers are excluded; AI material is licensed only insofar as you possess licensable rights; software can retain MIT or another software license; music/art can remain separately governed.

There's an interesting wrinkle here, though. **CC BY already permits commercial use provided its attribution requirements are satisfied.** That may actually be almost exactly what you're asking for at the copyright level.

The remaining word in your formulation is *consolidation*. We need to define what you mean by that very carefully before drafting anything, because it could mean several legally different things: acknowledgment of intellectual provenance, citation of specific prior formulations, disclosure that a commercial derivative was developed from SAT, preservation of modification history, or some form of reciprocal sharing.

My reading of what you've said so far is that you **don't particularly want reciprocal open-sourcing**. You want commercial users who actually derive material from the archive to **not erase the trail back to the source**.

If that's right, we're much closer to **BY than BY-NC or BY-SA**.

And I'd preserve MIT specifically for the archive tools. That's exactly what MIT is good at. The mistake wasn't choosing MIT for software; it was apparently putting a software license at the root of a giant heterogeneous intellectual archive.

One thing I would do before touching `LICENSE`: make a tag/release of the repository exactly as it exists now. That permanently fixes the old-license state and the contents to which it was attached. Then the new rights policy can begin with the next archive release, rather than trying to use access dates.

I would **not change the repository yet**. We should first settle precisely what “commercialization without consolidation” means to you, because I now think that's the key to choosing between ordinary CC BY and a custom additional condition. memcite

a request for common decency and professional courtesy. If Google turns holonomy into ubiquitous teleporter booths and immediate obsolescence of all other vehicles, and done so in a way that's recognizably SAT-shaped... I think it's within my rights to ask them to either make that free and accessible to everyone (including me), or at least maybe a tip or small accolade somewhere between "your idea seems to be useful in our dev and continue to make our technical reports available free to all" and "we've turned this idea of yours into a multibillion dollar market and we graceously accept your generous intellectual endowment, re-presenting it as though it were ours". 

I'm not sure what's usually expected, nor what height of stupidity I'd be accused of if it turned out I've just handed out something that turns out to be magic beans to industries that are perfectly happy to monetize mother nature while respecting my ethical boundaries by accepting my apparent opt-out of even nominal remuneration.

Yes. I would make this a short repository-level notice that **incorporates CC BY-NC 4.0 rather than trying to rewrite the CC license itself**. Creative Commons recommends using the standard license; BY-NC permits redistribution and adaptation for noncommercial purposes with attribution. citeturn0search3turn0search13

Here's the draft I'd start from. This is a practical draft, not legal advice, and I'd have counsel review it before treating it as final.

:::writing{variant="document" id="68417"}
# SAT / RMS / H(s)H Research Archive — License and Rights Notice

**Effective for new releases beginning August 31, 2026**

Copyright © Nathan Joseph Bellomy. All rights reserved except as expressly licensed below.

## 1. License

Except where otherwise identified in this notice or in an individual file, copyrightable material in the SAT / RMS / H(s)H Research Archive for which Nathan Joseph Bellomy holds the necessary rights is made available under the **Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC 4.0).**

The official CC BY-NC 4.0 license governs the permissions granted under that license.

In practical terms, this permits copying, redistribution, quotation, analysis, adaptation, translation, formalization, computational implementation of copyrightable expression, and the creation of derivative works for **noncommercial purposes**, subject to the attribution and other requirements of CC BY-NC 4.0.

Commercial rights are reserved. Commercial use may be separately licensed by the rights holder.

## 2. Attribution

Where reasonably practicable, attribution should identify:

**Nathan Joseph Bellomy**  
**SAT / RMS / H(s)H Research Archive**

and should identify or link to the specific document, archive release, repository version, commit, recording, or other source used when that information is available.

Where material has been modified, reconstructed, translated, formalized, summarized, or otherwise adapted, the resulting work must not be represented as Nathan Bellomy's original wording or original formulation without qualification.

Nothing in this notice requires an author to imply endorsement, collaboration, or agreement by Nathan Bellomy.

## 3. Scope of the Archive

The archive documents a continuing research and development program encompassing **RMS, Scalar-Angular-Torsion (SAT), H(s)H**, associated mathematical and computational work, methodological development, philosophical and epistemological work, simulations, diagrams, recordings, research notes, and related materials.

A substantial portion of the archive consists of extended human–AI conversations and materials produced through iterative human direction, criticism, selection, correction, reconstruction, formalization, calculation, simulation, and research.

For purposes of this archive, inclusion within the SAT / RMS / H(s)H research corpus does **not** constitute a representation that Nathan Bellomy personally authored every sentence, equation, image, or other expressive element contained in every file.

## 4. Human and AI Contributions

Nathan Bellomy is the human originator and principal director of the SAT / RMS / H(s)H research program represented by this archive.

The archive contains material produced with assistance from multiple artificial-intelligence systems, including ChatGPT/OpenAI models, Gemini and NotebookLM systems, Claude/Anthropic models, and other systems where identified in the historical record.

Such systems have been used for purposes including mathematical formalization, calculation, simulation, criticism, literature research, interpretation, drafting, reconstruction, and methodological experimentation.

Speaker attribution in historical conversation exports is sometimes incomplete. Labels such as **Nathan**, **User**, or equivalent designations generally identify Nathan Bellomy where the surrounding record establishes that attribution. Absence of a speaker label should not by itself be understood as an assertion concerning authorship.

This license applies to AI-assisted or AI-containing materials only to the extent that Nathan Bellomy possesses copyright or other rights capable of being licensed. No claim of copyright is made merely by virtue of an AI-generated item appearing in this archive.

## 5. Scientific Ideas, Mathematics, Facts, and Priority

This license governs copyright and related rights in covered material. It does **not** purport to establish ownership through copyright of scientific ideas, discoveries, facts, mathematical truths, physical principles, methods, or other subject matter outside the scope of copyright protection.

Likewise, this license does not itself establish scientific validity, correctness, novelty, or priority.

The archive's dates, recordings, drawings, commits, conversations, publications, version histories, and other provenance records are preserved as evidence from which the historical development and chronology of particular concepts may independently be evaluated.

Permission to use material under this license should not be interpreted as abandonment or waiver of claims concerning historical attribution or priority that may be supported by that record.

## 6. Third-Party Material

The archive may contain papers, excerpts, images, datasets, quotations, reference materials, or other works created by third parties.

**Third-party material is not licensed under this notice unless expressly stated otherwise.**

Copyright and other rights in such material remain with their respective rights holders. Inclusion in the archive should not be interpreted as an assertion of ownership by Nathan Bellomy or as permission to reuse that material beyond whatever rights otherwise apply.

Reasonable efforts will be made over time to improve identification and provenance labeling of such material.

## 7. Software and Code

Software source code may carry a separate software license identified in the relevant file or directory.

Where a separate software license is provided, that license governs the software code rather than CC BY-NC 4.0.

Research prose, documentation, conversation records, diagrams, datasets, or other materials stored alongside software are not automatically governed by the software license merely because they occupy the same repository.

## 8. Commercial Use

CC BY-NC 4.0 does not grant permission for uses that fall outside its NonCommercial limitation.

Nothing in this notice prevents Nathan Bellomy from granting separate commercial licenses, permissions, partnerships, or other arrangements for particular materials or applications.

Requests for commercial permission should identify the material and intended use.

## 9. Earlier Releases

Materials previously distributed under another license remain subject to rights already validly granted under the license applicable to those copies or releases.

This notice applies to materials **first released, or expressly designated as newly licensed, on or after August 31, 2026**, unless a particular file states otherwise.

For provenance purposes, the repository state immediately preceding this licensing transition should be preserved as a dated release or version-history boundary.

Later modification or republication of a previously released file does not by itself revoke permissions already granted for earlier copies under an earlier license.

## 10. No Endorsement or Warranty

Use of the archive, attribution to it, or permission granted under this license does not imply endorsement by Nathan Bellomy of a subsequent interpretation, theory, product, publication, formalization, or application.

The archive is a research record containing exploratory, historical, superseded, provisional, speculative, and unfinished material as well as material regarded by its author as current.

Materials are provided without warranty as to correctness, fitness for a particular purpose, scientific acceptance, or suitability for technical, medical, engineering, financial, safety-critical, or other applications.

## 11. Citation and Provenance

Researchers are strongly encouraged to cite the most specific available source and version rather than citing the archive generically.

Where a later SAT / RMS / H(s)H formulation can be traced to an earlier archived drawing, conversation, recording, document, or other source, preservation of that developmental provenance is encouraged.

The purpose of these provisions is not to prevent independent development, criticism, competing theories, reinterpretation, or scholarly use. It is to preserve a transparent historical record and make responsible reuse straightforward.

---

**License:** Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0)

**Effective date for this notice:** August 31, 2026

There are two things I deliberately **didn't** put into this draft.

I didn't say that AI-generated equations become your copyrighted works merely because you specifically directed their production. Current U.S. Copyright Office guidance is more cautious: AI assistance doesn't prevent copyright protection for a larger human-authored work, and human selection, arrangement or modification can matter, but copyrightability ultimately depends on sufficient human authorship of expressive elements. citeturn0search0turn0search24 The archive notice doesn't need to resolve that question; “to the extent I possess licensable rights” handles it cleanly.

I also didn't try to make attribution legally stronger than CC BY-NC itself by inventing a modified “CC BY-NC-SAT” license. That could create ambiguity about whether you're actually using CC BY-NC. The priority/provenance language instead explains what the archive is and requests good scientific practice without pretending copyright controls ideas.

One thing I'd consider changing before adoption is **Section 9**. We should look at your *current* archive license and its exact wording. Then I can make the transition clause precise rather than generic. memcite

parts:
I think there is a sane middle position here, and it is closer to what you're describing than either “everything is free forever” or “nobody commercial can touch this.”

The key is to separate **ordinary access and scientific use** from **large-scale closed commercial exploitation**.

Your citation idea is good precisely because it can be almost frictionless. I would give several equivalent suggested forms, from almost comically short to formal, and let the user choose one appropriate to the context. For example:

> **SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox, Nathan McKnight / Nathan J. Bellomy, [URL], accessed [date].**

Or the compact form:

> **SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox [URL], [access date].**

Or targeted:

> **Nathan McKnight, SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox, “[file/subsection],” [URL], accessed [date].**

Or, where provenance actually matters:

> **Nathan McKnight (Nathan J. Bellomy), RMS/SAT/H(s)H Research Archive — SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox, [specific artifact/version], [URL], accessed [date].**

That creates a nice gradient. Nobody has to write a historiographic essay merely because one SAT representation was useful. But somebody making a serious technical claim has an obvious way to point to the exact antecedent.

And I would explicitly say that **reasonable equivalent citation is acceptable**. You don't want someone technically violating the license because their journal citation style moves the access date three characters to the left.

On commercialization, I think I was still drawing the line too crudely with CC BY versus BY-NC.

What you want is approximately:

> **Free access and free scientific development. Small-scale commercialization is not the problem. Large, closed commercial appropriation is the point at which permission changes.**

There is precedent for that general licensing architecture, although mostly in software. Some licenses distinguish noncommercial from commercial use, permit trials, or provide alternate commercial licenses. Creative Commons itself explicitly permits **dual licensing**: for example, publishing under CC BY-NC while separately granting commercial permission to particular users. citeturn940994search4turn396515search4

I think that suggests a much cleaner solution for you than inventing one gigantic custom license:

**Base license: CC BY-NC 4.0.**  
Everyone automatically gets broad noncommercial rights to share, adapt and build on copyrightable archive material, subject to attribution. citeturn396515search1turn396515search4

Then publish a separate document called something like:

**SAT Open Commercial Permission**

That document grants *additional* permissions beyond BY-NC.

And that's where your actual ethics can live.

For instance, conceptually—not legal language yet:

> Commercial research, experimentation, teaching, criticism, prototyping and small-scale development are welcomed.
>
> Commercial use by individuals, independent researchers and small organizations is permitted without fee provided reasonable attribution to the archive is preserved.
>
> Larger commercial exploitation may alternatively qualify without payment where resulting research, methods, specifications or other substantial derivative knowledge are made openly available with appropriate provenance.
>
> Closed commercial exploitation beyond a stated scale requires separate permission from Nathan McKnight / Nathan J. Bellomy.

That is very close to what you just described.

It creates **two exits for Google-with-teleporters**:

**Pay something / make an arrangement**, or **give something substantial back to the commons**.

You aren't dictating Google's business model. You're saying: *I gave the commons this research freely. If you turn the protected material into a major private extraction mechanism, either maintain a meaningful commons relationship or come talk to me.*

That seems internally consistent with your position.

I would not use **market cXXXtalization** as the threshold, though. Market cap is a terrible metric for this: private companies don't have one; public valuations fluctuate wildly; and a trillion-dollar company could make $300 from SAT while a $2M startup could build its entire company around it.

Better candidates are:

- annual gross organizational revenue;
- revenue attributable to the relevant product/service;
- perhaps both, with a safe harbor.

For example—numbers purely for illustrating the architecture:

> Automatic commercial permission while the organization has <$5M annual gross revenue **or** the SAT-related product has generated <$250k lifetime gross revenue.

Above that, contact you.

You could make those thresholds quite generous. The purpose isn't to shake down a graduate student who incorporated an SAT diagram into a paid lecture. It's to create an unmistakable point at which **“we've built an actual business around this”** changes the relationship.

And you could explicitly waive the threshold for open/public-benefit uses:

> No commercial-license fee required where the relevant technical development, documentation, and results are released freely to the public under qualifying open terms.

That is the part I find most aligned with what you're saying. Money isn't actually your objection. **Privatizing an asymmetry extracted from a freely disclosed structure is.**

There is one hard legal boundary we should keep very visible.

Copyright licensing does **not** give you a monopoly on the underlying physics, geometry, mathematics or ideas. CC itself is explicit that its licenses govern copyright and certain related rights the licensor can grant, not patent or trademark rights. citeturn396515search4

So suppose the archive says:

> particular holonomy structure → mechanism X

and Google reads it, independently writes entirely new software and hardware, and builds your hypothetical teleporter without copying protected expression.

A copyright license by itself may not force them to pay you.

That's where the “magic beans” question becomes materially different.

If you believe some **not-yet-published developments could constitute patentable technologies**, uploading them publicly without first deciding whether to pursue patent protection can indeed give away options. In the U.S. there is a limited one-year inventor-disclosure grace regime, but public disclosure can be much more damaging to foreign rights; that is exactly where a patent attorney should examine the particular disclosure before publication. The USPTO also treats sufficiently accessible Internet publications as potential prior art. citeturn940994search1turn940994search3

That cuts both ways.

Your existing public archive may be useful as **defensive prior art**: a later applicant may have difficulty patenting something already sufficiently disclosed and publicly accessible there. The USPTO specifically says an electronic Internet publication can qualify as a printed publication when publicly accessible to people concerned with the art; nobody has to prove that someone actually read it. citeturn940994search1

But defensive publication means roughly:

**“Nobody should be able to monopolize what I've already taught the public.”**

It does *not* mean:

**“I retain the exclusive commercial right to everything I taught the public.”**

Those are nearly opposite patent strategies.

So, on your “how stupid would this be?” question: publishing openly was not inherently stupid. It purchased some things very effectively—timestamped public provenance, accessibility, possible prior-art effects, independent inspectability, and the possibility that somebody would actually engage with an unconventional body of work.

But **continuing to publish every newly operationalizable technological detail without deciding whether you ever want patent rights would be an avoidable strategic choice**, now that you're explicitly thinking about this issue.

And I don't think you need to suddenly patent SAT. That sounds financially and conceptually absurd at this scale. I mean something narrower: if someday a result crosses from

> “interesting geometric grammar”

into

> “here is a reproducible device/process with an economically significant new capability,”

flag that item **before** putting the enabling details into the public archive.

There's another important reason your geometric grammar matters.

A single equation may have ambiguous ancestry. A whole recurring representational grammar—particular objects, transformations, dependency structure, characteristic explanatory moves, and then a technology reproducing a distinctive cluster of those things—is much more useful **evidentially** when asking whether later work plausibly descended from SAT.

It still doesn't magically create legal ownership of a scientific idea.

But it can make the provenance question much less fuzzy.

So I think the archive should actually state that distinction very calmly:

> The archive's citation request concerns not only verbatim text but recognizable substantive use of the RMS/SAT/H(s)H representational framework, terminology, diagrams, explanatory grammar, computational materials, or other attributable project materials. Nothing in this statement asserts copyright ownership over facts, mathematical truths, laws of nature, or independently developed ideas.

That tells people what you consider good scientific behavior without pretending copyright law reaches farther than it does.

My current preference, therefore, is:

**CC BY-NC 4.0 + a generous standing commercial-permission document + several extremely easy citation forms + third-party exclusions + separate MIT licensing for actual software.**

And above some meaningful commercial threshold, the standing permission can say essentially:

**choose openness or contact Nathan.**

That captures your teleport-booth example far better than either plain CC BY or an indiscriminate “NO COMMERCIAL USE” sign.

One caution: once we decide the actual threshold and conditions, I'd have an IP lawyer spend an hour reviewing **that commercial-permission document**, particularly because you have mixed copyrightable expression, database-like compilation, software, AI output and scientific ideas. We don't need them to invent your policy; we'd be handing them the policy and asking them to make sure the machinery actually says what you mean. memcite
